title: Form 10-K Cover
summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Form 10-K is its annual report for the year ended December 31, 2025. It identifies the company, its Delaware incorporation, New York headquarters, tax ID, and registered common, preferred depositary, and guaranteed note/ETN securities and exchanges. It reports filing and interactive-data compliance, large accelerated filer status, auditor attestation of internal-control effectiveness, and that it is not a shell company; it notes no registered Section 12(g) securities or indicated restatements. The filing gives common-stock market value and shares outstanding and incorporates specified portions of the 2026 proxy statement for Part III items.

title: Form 10-K Index
summary: This is a Form 10-K table of contents covering Parts I–IV: business overview, segments, competition, regulation, human capital, financial asset/liability and interest-rate information, risk factors, staff comments, cybersecurity, properties, legal proceedings, mine safety, stock matters, management’s discussion, market-risk disclosures, financial statements, accounting matters, controls, other disclosures, governance, executive compensation, beneficial ownership, related-party transactions, auditor fees, and exhibits and financial statement schedules.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business.
JPMorganChase Overview and Business Segments
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase is a Delaware financial holding company headquartered in the U.S., operating globally across banking, investment banking, payments and asset management. As of December 31, 2025, it had $4.4 trillion in assets and $362.4 billion in equity. The page describes its customers, principal U.S. and international subsidiaries, and website availability of SEC filings and investor information, noting website content is not incorporated into filings. Its reportable segments are Consumer & Community Banking, Commercial & Investment Bank, and Asset & Wealth Management; other activities are in Corporate. Segment and Corporate details appear in the MD&A and Note 32.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase operates in highly competitive markets against a broad range of financial institutions, technology firms and other providers of similar or emerging services. Competition is based on product and service quality and variety, execution, innovation, reputation and price, and differs by customers, industries, geographies and whether markets are global, national or regional. New entrants include internet-only firms and non-financial companies that disintermediate traditional banking services.

Holding company as a source of strength
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is extensively regulated in the U.S. and abroad, and industry legal challenges may change regulations’ scope, requirements or timing. The Federal Reserve supervises the holding company on a consolidated basis, alongside activity- and jurisdiction-specific regulators for subsidiaries. The text covers limits on BHC/FHC activities and consequences of eligibility or Community Reinvestment Act failures; capital, liquidity and leverage rules, including evolving Basel III proposals and implementation timelines; annual supervisory and company stress tests, capital plans and buffers, proposed framework changes, and a stayed legal challenge; enhanced prudential standards and the holding company’s duty to support banks; acquisition approvals, limits and notices; and a March 2024 OCC consent order concerning trading-venue inventories and trade-surveillance data.

nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory obligations across subsidiary banking, consumer protection, securities and broker-dealer activities, investment management, and derivatives. It covers OCC enforcement and bank governance; FDIC insurance, insolvency powers, and reserve targets; capital and dividend restrictions, affiliate transactions, and depositor priority; U.S., EU, and U.K. consumer oversight and pending data-access and interchange-fee rules; securities conduct and capital regulation; investment-adviser duties and a stayed DOL fiduciary rule; and swap-dealer registration and related derivatives requirements.

nodes.title: Consumer, Securities, and Investment Regulation
nodes.summary: The text covers U.S. consumer-data and debit-interchange rules and litigation, state interchange laws, and U.K. retail banking and investment regulation, including planned consolidation of the PSR into the FCA. It describes broker-dealer oversight and requirements in the U.S. and abroad, including market-conduct rules, and global asset and wealth management regulation, fiduciary duties, client-asset safeguards, and fund marketing. It also notes court stays and possible revisions affecting proposed CFPB and DOL rules.

nodes.title: Derivatives regulation:
nodes.summary: The Firm faces extensive global regulation across derivatives, data privacy, cybersecurity, AI, anti-money-laundering, sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation, and sustainability. Derivatives rules cover capital, collateral, segregation, conduct, clearing, trading, records, reporting, and market abuse. BSA requirements include risk controls, reporting, and customer due diligence; sanctions regimes may conflict across jurisdictions. Compensation oversight aims to curb imprudent risk-taking and continues to evolve. EU sustainability rules CSRD and CSDDD impose expanded reporting and phased-in human-rights and environmental due diligence obligations, with implementation delays and impacts across Firm entities.

nodes.summary: The text covers derivatives clearing, trading, reporting and anti-manipulation requirements across the U.S., EU, U.K. and other jurisdictions. It outlines evolving global rules on data, privacy, cybersecurity and AI; anti-money-laundering, record-keeping, due diligence and economic sanctions obligations; anti-corruption laws; and regulatory oversight of compensation practices, including incentive-risk standards and differing international rules.

nodes.title: Sustainability:
nodes.summary: U.K. and EU policymakers continue developing sustainability initiatives and disclosure rules. The EU’s CSRD expanded ESG reporting requirements, phased in from fiscal year 2024, though national implementation has been delayed in some member states, including Germany; the Firm monitors developments and potential impacts. Enacted in July 2024, the CSDDD introduces phased requirements from 2029, requiring companies to address actual and potential human rights violations and environmental harms in their operations and business relationships. Both directives affect certain Firm entities inside and outside the EU.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s extensive U.S. and international oversight of its holding company and subsidiaries, including regulator roles, activity restrictions, approvals, enforcement and governance. Covers capital, liquidity, leverage, stress tests, buffers, bank support, deposit insurance, dividends, affiliate transactions and depositor priority. Summarizes consumer, securities, broker-dealer, investment-management and derivatives rules; data access, interchange fees, fiduciary duties and client protections; and evolving global requirements for clearing, trading, reporting, privacy, cybersecurity, AI, anti-money-laundering, sanctions, anti-corruption and compensation. Also addresses EU and U.K. sustainability disclosure and due-diligence obligations, implementation timelines, proposed-rule changes, litigation and regulatory actions.

nodes.title: Human Capital
key_items: Attracting and retaining employees; Developing employees
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase says long-term success depends on attracting, developing, retaining and engaging talent in an inclusive workplace; reported workforce data excludes contractors. At year-end 2025, it had 318,512 employees in 66 countries, 58% in the U.S., with regional and business-line distributions provided. The text reports self-identified workforce diversity measures for employees, senior leaders, the Operating Committee and Board, with definitions, coverage and exclusions explained in footnotes. It describes skills-based recruiting and career opportunities, employee training and development, mandatory policy training, and market-competitive, performance-oriented compensation that incorporates risk and controls, alongside benefits and wellness support.

JPMorganChase’s business section outlines its global financial holding-company operations, scale, subsidiaries, investor-information disclosures and reportable segments. It describes competition from financial institutions, technology firms and new entrants, and extensive U.S. and international regulation across prudential, consumer, securities, markets, data, conduct and sustainability matters, including evolving rules and enforcement. It also covers workforce size and distribution, diversity measures, talent recruitment and development, training, compensation, benefits and wellness.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
Summary
key_items: The above summary is subject in its entirety to the discussion of the risk factors set forth below.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase warns that the listed risks are not exhaustive and could individually or jointly materially harm its business, earnings, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation. Risks include legal and regulatory burdens, uneven rules, governmental policies, litigation and enforcement, resolution-related creditor losses, political uncertainty, market volatility, credit and liquidity constraints, capital requirements, operational and cyber failures, strategy and competition, climate change, employee misconduct, reputation, country conditions and talent retention. The text defines key terms and details legal/regulatory risks: compliance costs and business restrictions; competitive disadvantages and conflicting laws; litigation, penalties and remediation; unpredictable jurisdictions and government policies; resolution-plan requirements; and loss allocation in a parent-company resolution. Political developments may disrupt economies, markets and client credit. Market risks affect consumer and wholesale activity, interest income, funding, asset values, fees, real estate exposures and hedging. Credit risks arise from client, counterparty, CCP, collateral, sovereign and market-participant failures, fraud, disputes and cascading disruption.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase could suffer losses if the value of collateral declines.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase may incur losses and increased credit risk if collateral values decline or cannot be realized, particularly during market stress or illiquidity. Risks include collateral sales failing to cover amounts owed, counterparties being unable to post collateral, borrowers failing to maintain or misrepresenting collateral, competing claims at liquidation, and valuation disputes. Losses may result if the firm cannot realize collateral’s fair value or manage value declines.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk.
JPMorganChase’s ability to operate its businesses could be impaired if its liquidity is constrained.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorganChase’s risks from concentrated and interconnected credit and market exposures, economic and industry downturns, consumer lending competition and defaults, private-credit stress, and inability to exit positions during market dislocations, which may increase losses, reserves, RWAs, funding costs, and reduce capital and profitability. Liquidity risks include market disruption, policy changes, asset-sale constraints, participant defaults, outflows, deposit losses, commitment draws, and confidence declines; alternative or regulatory funding may be costly or limited. The parent holding company depends on regulated subsidiaries for payments, and restrictions could prompt earlier resolution. Credit-rating downgrades could restrict business, raise costs and collateral needs, and reduce counterparties. Regulatory capital requirements may constrain shareholder distributions and business support; the text begins describing factors that may increase required capital.

nodes.title: Liquidity, Funding, Ratings, and Capital Risks
key_items: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a holding company and depends on its subsidiaries for funding to make payments on its outstanding securities.
JPMorganChase’s liquidity and cost of funding could be adversely affected by downgrades in its credit ratings.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from market stress and reduced access to stable funding, potentially requiring more costly or limited alternatives, and warns that weak liquidity management or regulatory requirements could constrain operations. As a holding company, JPMorgan Chase & Co. relies on subsidiaries for payments on its securities; regulatory limits on subsidiary dividends and lending could leave it unable to meet obligations or lead to earlier resolution. Credit-rating downgrades could restrict market access, raise costs and collateral needs, reduce counterparties, and lower debt values. Regulatory capital requirements may also limit shareholder distributions and business support, and required capital can increase.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s ability to distribute capital to shareholders, and to support its business activities could be limited if it does not satisfy applicable regulatory capital requirements.
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorganChase risks involving limited or costly alternative funding during market stress, regulatory liquidity demands, and inadequate liquidity management; the Parent Company’s dependence on regulated subsidiary dividends and IHC borrowing to meet obligations, with restrictions potentially prompting earlier resolution or bankruptcy; and credit downgrades that could raise funding costs, restrict market access, trigger collateral needs, and reduce counterparties. Capital-rule changes or shortfalls could constrain shareholder distributions and business activity. Operational-system failures, cyber threats, data or connectivity problems, and third-party disruptions can harm customers and the firm; ongoing complexity and evolving fraud make prevention and resilience challenging.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s businesses could be adversely affected by the failure or disruption of operational systems on which they depend.
nodes.summary: The text explains that regulatory actions, legal changes, balance-sheet shifts, rising risk-weighted assets or stress losses may increase JPMorganChase’s capital requirements. Falling below requirements or using capital buffers can restrict distributions and bonuses, harm shareholders through limits on buybacks, capital instruments, dividends, or business activity. It also describes operational-system risks: failures, cyberattacks, data and technology issues, and third-party outages; factors that hinder resilience; prior customer impacts; and possible service, transaction, financial, market, legal, and reputational consequences.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s interconnectedness with clients, customers and other external parties could be a source of significant operational risk.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s growing reliance on interconnected clients, customers, third parties, and financial-market infrastructure creates operational risks from system failures, cyberattacks, human error, or misconduct—especially in external systems and internet, cloud, or mobile activities beyond its control. Such events may require protective measures, including restricting account access, raising costs and reducing customer confidence. Disruptions at interconnected financial entities can spread industry-wide and materially impair JPMorganChase’s business, particularly when affected third-party services are widely used.

nodes.title: A successful cyber attack could cause significant harm to JPMorganChase and its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces frequent and evolving cyber attacks from state-backed actors, criminals and hacktivists, targeting systems, data, services and money through malware, unauthorized access, disruption, theft and ransomware. Past breaches have occurred and future ones are inevitable; detection and prevention cannot be guaranteed because attacks are sophisticated, persistent, diverse, and may exploit third parties. Geopolitical tensions, AI, quantum computing and outdated protections heighten risks, requiring costly security upgrades that may lag threats. Vulnerabilities include access controls, software, vendors, asset inventories, DDoS and recovery capabilities, cloud migration, network connections, insider threats and acquired-business integration. Third-party breaches, including interception of employees’ mobile communications, may also expose the firm. Consequences include outages, data theft, fraud, ransom demands, legal or privacy violations, uncovered financial losses, litigation, penalties, lost confidence and reputational harm. Investigations and remediation may be prolonged and uncertain, allowing damage to spread, complicating communications and increasing costs.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s businesses could be adversely affected if it fails to identify and address operational risks associated with the introduction of or changes to products, services, delivery platforms or technologies.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase may fail to recognize or control operational risks arising from new or changed products, services, delivery platforms, businesses, acquisitions or integrations, investments, and technologies. Inadequate risk identification or controls could disrupt operations, create liability, impair liquidity and competitiveness, increase compliance, operational, integration, litigation, or penalty costs, trigger regulatory intervention, cause fraud losses, and damage its reputation—materially harming its businesses and results.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s business and operations rely on appropriate staffing and on the competence, trustworthiness, health and safety of employees.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s efficient and profitable operations, client offerings, and risk management depend on adequate staffing and employees’ competence, trustworthiness, health, and safety, as well as on third-party and potential acquisition workforces. Operations may be harmed by labor shortages, failure to follow controls, workforce disruption from health emergencies or other extraordinary events, employee theft, fraud or unlawful conduct, human error or misconduct, or ineffective health and safety measures by the firm, government authorities, or other relied-upon parties.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase faces substantial legal and operational risks related to the processing and safeguarding of personal information.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces legal, operational, financial, and reputational risks from handling personal information under global privacy laws. Compliance may limit products, pricing, data transfers, and efficient operations, increase costs, or create conflicts between jurisdictions. Mishandling data, security failures by the bank or vendors, or perceived noncompliance could trigger investigations, enforcement, penalties, operational changes, and loss of customers or employees. Sophisticated identity fraud may cause unauthorized transactions and losses. Increasing government scrutiny and stricter future laws could raise compliance costs and constrain services.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s operations, results and reputation could be harmed by occurrences of extraordinary events beyond its control.
nodes.summary: Extraordinary events beyond JPMorganChase’s control—including cyber or physical security incidents, utility, communications, technology or third-party service failures, property damage, legal noncompliance by related parties, natural disasters and climate effects, accidents, health emergencies, and violence or civil unrest—could disrupt operations and harm its reputation. Its resiliency framework may not prevent, anticipate or manage all, especially simultaneous, prolonged or chronic disruptions; geographic concentration or dispersion of personnel, assets and providers may impede response. Disruptions could impede services and transactions, require costly remediation, cause losses, liabilities, injuries, market-infrastructure interruptions, litigation, penalties and reputational damage. They may also weaken clients’ and customers’ finances, increase credit-loss allowances and charge-offs, and reduce earnings.

nodes.title: Any failure to maintain adequate data management processes could adversely affect JPMorganChase’s ability to effectively manage its businesses, comply with applicable law or make informed business decisions.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorganChase’s risks from inadequate data management, including impaired risk, fraud, cybersecurity, compliance, reporting, business and customer-service functions, and possible losses, costs, regulatory failures and reputational damage; data theft could enable fraud. It also describes costs and exposures from failing to oversee vendors and service providers, and consequences of weaknesses in risk management, governance, models, reporting or controls. Finally, it explains model and estimation limitations—including uncertain or changing conditions, data or technology errors, valuation challenges and flawed review—that could cause unexpected losses, reduce capital and increase regulatory scrutiny.

nodes.title: Vendor Oversight and Risk Management Exposures
key_items: Enhanced regulatory and other standards for the oversight of JPMorganChase’s vendors and other service providers could result in higher costs and other potential exposures.
JPMorganChase could incur losses arising from any significant inadequacy or lapse in its risk management framework and control environment.
nodes.summary: Enhanced standards for overseeing vendors, service providers, outsourcing, and subsidiary functions may increase costs and expose JPMorganChase to customer harm and liability, lost revenue, operational costs, penalties, and reputational damage if relationships are poorly managed. Significant weaknesses in risk management, governance, models, reporting, or controls could impair risk identification and escalation, lead to harmful decisions, customer losses, remediation costs, legal noncompliance, regulatory scrutiny, litigation, investigations, penalties, and reputational harm, adversely affecting financial condition or results.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase could recognize unexpected losses, its capital levels could be reduced and it could face greater regulatory scrutiny if its models, estimations or judgments, including those used in its financial statements, are inadequate or incorrect.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase relies on models, estimates, and judgments for risk management and U.S. GAAP reporting, based on historical data and assumptions that are periodically revised. They may fail because trends change, forecasts are inherently uncertain, data are incomplete or biased, markets become illiquid, technology or inputs are flawed, or reviews miss errors. Inadequate estimates—including fair values and credit-loss allowances based on management judgment and economic forecasts—can cause unexpected losses, reduce capital, and invite regulatory scrutiny. Regulators must approve certain Basel III risk-weighted-asset models; rejection could increase capital charges, harm results, or constrain business growth.

nodes.title: A significant inadequacy in disclosure or financial reporting controls could negatively affect JPMorganChase’s business, operations and reputation.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s complex global reporting obligations and potentially ineffective disclosure controls could lead to inaccurate reporting, harming its business, finances, market access and reputation, and causing remediation costs, litigation or penalties. Its results and competitiveness also depend on management developing and executing sound strategies across products, markets, customers, investments, counterparties, technology and delivery channels. Poor choices, information, planning or responses to competitive, regulatory, market and stakeholder changes could weaken growth and earnings. Key execution needs include effective plans and offerings, prudent capital allocation and investment oversight, acquisition due diligence and integration, stakeholder engagement, risk management, responsiveness, workforce planning and capabilities to manage growth. Costs from asset disposals or business and product exits may also be material.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s results or competitive standing could suffer if its management fails to develop and execute effective business strategies and to anticipate changes affecting those strategies.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from model uncertainty and regulatory approval requirements for Basel III risk-weighted assets, including potentially higher capital charges if models are rejected. It warns that ineffective disclosure or financial-reporting controls could cause inaccurate reporting, harming results, market access, resources, and reputation, or leading to litigation and penalties. It also describes strategic risks: poor planning or execution, misjudged markets, inadequate investment and acquisition decisions, weak stakeholder response or risk management, slow adaptation to change and AI, and insufficient capabilities could undermine competitiveness, growth, earnings, expense control, and shareholder returns; exiting businesses or disposing of assets may also be costly.

nodes.title: Competition in the financial services industry could lead to negative effects on JPMorganChase’s results of operations.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces intense, evolving competition from financial institutions and technology and other nonbank firms, enabled by e-commerce and advances in online lending, payments, cryptocurrency and stablecoins, tokenized securities, automated investment advice, and distributed-ledger technology that may bypass intermediaries. Keeping pace, including with generative AI, may require greater investment; falling behind could cost clients and market share, while disruptive, misused, or breached technologies could raise compliance costs and reduce income. Competitors may pressure prices, capture market share, or seek regulatory exemptions that disadvantage banks. Failure to meet customer expectations, additional capital needs, and uncertain or inconsistent technology regulation could reduce revenues, increase costs, restrict offerings, or forfeit opportunities.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s operations, results, and competitive standing could be adversely affected by the development of advanced technologies such as AI.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to JPMorganChase from advanced technologies, especially AI: system errors, misuse, bias, privacy and security failures, cyber threats, regulatory costs, competitive disadvantage, loss of direct customer relationships, and poor workforce planning or adoption. Climate change poses physical and transition risks that may affect assets, costs, clients, creditworthiness, markets, and strategy. Employee misconduct may cause litigation, enforcement, penalties, higher costs, and reputational harm, particularly in acquired businesses. Reputation can also suffer from business decisions, misinformation (including AI-generated content), or perceived unfair treatment, leading to scrutiny, investigations, litigation, and adverse media. These risks could damage business, operations, results, competitive standing, and prospects.

nodes.title: AI, Climate, Conduct and Reputation Risks
key_items: The effects of climate change could adversely affect JPMorganChase’s business and operations, both directly and as a result of impacts on its clients and customers.
Conduct failure by JPMorganChase employees could trigger litigation and regulatory actions and harm JPMorganChase’s reputation.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from AI-related competitive disadvantages, customer disintermediation, and workforce planning or skills gaps; climate change’s physical and transition effects on JPMorganChase and its clients; employee misconduct leading to legal, regulatory, operational and reputational consequences, including at acquired businesses; and reputational harm from business decisions, misinformation, or perceived unfair treatment, potentially prompting scrutiny, investigations, litigation, and adverse media coverage.

nodes.title: Damage to JPMorganChase’s reputation could negatively affect its business, results and prospects.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from ineffective or excessive AI use, including competitive losses, weakened customer relationships, workforce skills gaps, and adverse effects on JPMorganChase. Climate-related physical and transition risks may disrupt operations, reduce asset values, raise costs, and impair clients and strategy. Employee misconduct and reputational damage can trigger legal, regulatory, financial, and business consequences. Failure to manage conflicts of interest, fiduciary duties, service standards, or confidential information may cause penalties and lost revenue. International hostilities may disrupt markets, trade, infrastructure, currencies, and operations, while local economic, political, regulatory, and social conditions can also threaten business in certain countries.

nodes.title: Conflicts of Interest and Geopolitical Hostilities
key_items: Failure to effectively manage potential conflicts of interest or to satisfy fiduciary obligations could result in litigation and enforcement actions and cause reputational harm.

An outbreak or escalation of hostilities between countries or within a country or region could have a material adverse effect on the global economy and on JPMorganChase’s businesses within the affected region or globally.
nodes.summary: The text describes how failures to manage conflicts of interest, meet fiduciary duties, serve clients fairly, disclose conflicts, or protect confidential information can lead to customer losses, litigation, penalties, regulatory scrutiny, lost revenue, higher costs, and reputational harm. It also explains how escalating hostilities could trigger cyberattacks, war, economic and market disruption, asset and currency declines, infrastructure and trade interruptions, sanctions, and humanitarian crises, harming JPMorganChase’s global operations and earnings, potentially requiring it to curtail operations.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s business and operations in certain countries could be adversely affected by local economic, political, regulatory and social factors.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s operations in countries with volatile economies, less-established or unpredictable institutions, and significant government control may be harmed by economic disruptions such as currency swings, inflation, weak growth, sovereign debt problems, and fraud. Government responses—including price, capital, or exchange controls, property confiscation or blocked access, and legal changes—may further damage business, especially in small, illiquid markets. Unrest, crime, corruption, safety threats, conflict, political overthrow, terrorism, and other instability can impair operations, revenues, growth, and profitability; events in one country may also affect operations and investments elsewhere, including the U.S.

JPMorganChase faces concentrated credit and market risks, including downturns, defaults, private-credit stress and illiquid positions, which can increase losses, funding costs and capital needs. Market disruption, outflows, subsidiary-payment restrictions, ratings downgrades and higher capital rules may constrain liquidity, operations, distributions and growth. Operational threats include system, cyber, third-party and infrastructure failures; new-product and technology risks; staffing, privacy, data, vendor, risk-control, model, reporting and disclosure weaknesses; extraordinary events; and poor strategic execution. Competition, AI, climate change, misconduct, reputational damage, conflicts of interest, geopolitical hostilities, and local economic, political, regulatory and social instability may also harm customers, operations, earnings and prospects.

nodes.title: People Various factors could impact JPMorganChase’s workforce.
nodes.summary: The text outlines workforce risks from skills needs, competitor poaching, leadership succession, immigration and travel restrictions, and technology-driven displacement, potentially affecting performance, costs, efficiency, training, morale, and retention. It reports no unresolved staff comments, refers readers to the management discussion for cybersecurity risks, and describes the firm’s headquarters and owned or leased properties by region, totaling 74.2 million square feet, including 5,083 U.S. branches. It notes shared property use, ongoing space reviews, possible disposal costs, and a vacant New York building under remodeling. Material legal proceedings are referenced in Note 30; mine safety disclosures are not applicable.

JPMorganChase describes a broad, non-exhaustive range of risks that could materially affect its business, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness or reputation. These include legal, regulatory, political, market, credit, collateral, concentration, liquidity and capital risks; operational, cyber, technology, third-party, model and strategic failures; competition, climate change, misconduct, conflicts, reputation and geopolitical or local instability. The section also covers workforce and talent risks, cybersecurity cross-references, real-estate holdings and property costs, material legal proceedings, and the inapplicability of mine-safety disclosures.

It describes JPMorganChase’s owned, fully occupied New York headquarters and its owned or leased facilities across U.S. locations, noting shared use, ongoing space reviews, and potential costs or uncertainty from disposing of excess properties. It refers to occupancy expense details and to Note 30 for material legal proceedings.

Management, including the CEO and CFO, evaluated disclosure controls and concluded they were effective; their certifications are in Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2. The Firm notes inherent control limitations and the possibility of future deficiencies or material weaknesses. No change during the quarter materially affected, or was reasonably likely to materially affect, internal control over financial reporting.

nodes.title: Item 9B. Other Information.
nodes.summary: The filing reports fourth-quarter 2025 Rule 10b5-1 plans adopted by ten Section 16 directors or officers, listing their roles, adoption dates, durations, and shares to be sold. Sales generally involve 50% of net shares from March 2026 PSU vesting; other specified amounts are 200,000, 865, and 50,000 shares. It notes cooling-off and share-count conditions, trust transactions for Dimon and Lake, and no other plans adopted or any plans terminated. Iran disclosures describe three exempt, fee-free payments of about $130 each to the Iranian Embassy for a client’s children’s travel documents, and an account held by an employee of an Iranian-government-controlled entity, generating about $850 in fees on an approximately $119,000 balance before closure. The Firm knows of no other reportable 2025 activity and does not intend future such transactions.

nodes.title: Provision for credit losses
nodes.summary: The table reports provisions for credit losses (in millions) for 2023–2025: total provisions of $9.3 billion, $10.7 billion, and $14.2 billion, respectively, broken down by consumer (including credit card), wholesale, and investment securities. In 2025, net charge-offs were $9.8 billion and the allowance increased by $4.4 billion. Consumer provision was $11.5 billion, reflecting $8.3 billion of charge-offs and a $3.3 billion allowance addition, driven by the Apple Card transaction, Card Services loan growth, and macroeconomic outlook changes, partly offset by reduced borrower uncertainty. Wholesale provision was $2.7 billion, reflecting portfolio growth, client-specific credit changes, revised leveraged-loan assumptions, and estimated fraud losses, partly offset by macroeconomic changes; wholesale charge-offs and allowance addition were $1.6 billion and $1.1 billion. In 2024, provision was $10.7 billion, charge-offs $8.6 billion, and allowance addition $2.0 billion. The text directs readers to segment results, allowance disclosures, critical accounting estimates, and Notes 12–13 for further information.

Selected Consolidated balance sheets data
nodes.summary: The text analyzes JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated balance-sheet changes from December 31, 2024 to 2025, noting total assets rose 11% to $4.425 trillion and referring readers to critical accounting estimates and related notes. Cash and bank deposits fell due to Markets activity, investment and loan growth, and Treasury/CIO cash deployment, partly offset by deposits and debt. Federal funds/resale agreements, securities borrowed, and trading assets increased with Markets activity and client demand. Investment securities rose through AFS purchases, partly offset by maturities; a $44.1 billion AFS-to-HTM transfer occurred, while HTM declined with maturities. Loans grew in wholesale, securities-based, and card lending, partly offset by Home Lending declines. Loan-loss allowances rose $1.4 billion, including $1.1 billion consumer and $350 million wholesale additions; lending-commitment allowances also increased $3.0 billion, mainly due to the Apple Card transaction and new commitments. Receivables increased with Markets activity; premises and equipment rose with property investments; other assets increased from Markets collateral and auto lease assets. Goodwill and intangible assets are referenced to notes.

nodes.title: Consolidated cash flows analysis
nodes.summary: The text analyzes JPMorganChase’s consolidated cash flows for 2025, 2024 and 2023, referring readers elsewhere for discussion of 2023. It reports net cash from or used in operating, investing and financing activities, exchange-rate effects, and overall cash changes. Operating cash use in 2025 reflected growth in trading assets, securities borrowed, loans held for sale, other assets, and receivables, partly offset by adjusted net income and higher trading liabilities; 2024 use mainly reflected trading assets and securities borrowed. Investing cash use in both years came from loan originations, securities purchases and resale agreements, with 2024 partly offset by loan-sale and securitization proceeds. Financing cash provided in 2025 reflected deposit growth, repo-related funding and borrowings; in 2024, repo funding and borrowings were partly offset by preferred-stock redemptions. Both years included common-stock repurchases and common and preferred dividends. The Firm says operating liquidity is adequate and directs readers to related balance-sheet, capital-risk, liquidity-risk and cash-flow-statement discussions.

Non-GAAP financial measures

Revenue sharing

nodes.title: Expense allocation
nodes.summary: The text explains how JPMorgan Chase allocates service costs to business segments based on use and actual cost, while retaining certain unused or non-segment-specific costs in Corporate. It describes FTP’s allocation of interest income and expense and transfer of interest-rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO, including a 2024 consumer-deposit methodology change offset in Corporate, lower funding costs, and deposit-margin compression. Foreign-exchange risks are centrally managed by Treasury and CIO. Most unsecured debt credit-spread costs and preferred dividends are allocated to segments based on regulatory capital and funding needs. Capital allocation uses Basel III RWA, the GSIB surcharge, and severe-stress depletion estimates, with methodology reassessed at least annually.

nodes.title: Funds Transfer Pricing and Financial Risk Allocation

Foreign-exchange risks are also centrally managed by Treasury and CIO. FTP allocates most unsecured long-term debt credit-spread costs and preferred stock dividends to segments, based on regulatory capital and funding needs, with debt costs included in net interest income and dividends deducted to determine net income applicable to common equity.

nodes.title: Firmwide Risk Management
Risk governance framework
key_items: Three lines of defense; Risk identification and ownership
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes its goal of balancing client and investor service with firm safety through shared risk responsibility, LOB and Corporate ownership, governance, and risk-aware compensation. Its framework considers risk drivers, four categories—strategic, credit and investment, market, and operational—and quantitative or qualitative consequences. Independent Risk Management, led by the CRO under Board Risk Committee oversight, establishes and oversees policies and standards. The three defense lines are business risk owners, independent Risk Management and Compliance, and Internal Audit; other functions also support controls. LOBs identify and control risks, while IRM challenges them and maintains an inventory. Senior management sets risk appetite, the Board Risk Committee approves it, and results are monitored and reported.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight structure

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight functions

Country Risk Management, for example, oversees country risk as a driver or an aggregation of exposures that may create credit or market risk. The document introduces sections on the Firm’s oversight functions and lists their page references: Strategic, Capital, Liquidity, Reputation, Consumer Credit, Wholesale Credit, Investment Portfolio, Market, Country, Climate, Operational, Compliance, Conduct, Legal, and Estimations and Model Risk.

nodes.title: Capital Risk Management
Capital planning and stress testing
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s capital risk philosophy: maintain a strong, liquid, resilient balance sheet and assess capital implications of major decisions. An independent Capital Risk Management function oversees metrics, limits, breaches, capital-management assessments, and regulatory compliance; Treasury and CIO manage capital to support investment, subsidiaries, regulatory requirements, distributions, and resolution readiness through internal minimums, flexibility, monitoring, and escalation. Governance involves several management committees and Board Risk Committee review. Annual Federal Reserve CCAR evaluates capital adequacy, planning, and distributions; the Firm’s SCB is 2.5% through September 30, 2027, and its standardized CET1 requirement was 11.5% at year-end 2025. The annual ICAAP integrates capital planning and stress tests, reviewed by the Audit Committee, using macroeconomic, market, operational-risk, tailored, and sensitivity scenarios.

nodes.title: Contingency Capital Plan
nodes.summary: The Contingency Capital Plan sets the Firm’s capital management framework and principles for normal and stressed conditions. It explains how targeted capital levels are calibrated, minimum capital requirements are met, planned distributions are monitored for ongoing appropriateness, and contingency actions are selected or considered as capital depletes under stress.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve sets consolidated capital standards for JPMorgan Chase, while the OCC sets standards for its principal bank; U.S. rules generally follow Basel. Basel III calculates risk-weighted assets (RWA) under Standardized and Advanced approaches, with capital adequacy assessed against the more binding applicable requirements. The approaches differ chiefly in credit-risk methods; Advanced also includes operational risk, while market-risk treatment is generally similar. Models, supervisory feedback, and management judgment can affect RWA. At year-end 2025, Advanced ratios became more binding, mainly due to Apple Card-related RWA increases and a lower Standardized-only stress capital buffer (SCB). Advanced banks also calculate supplementary leverage ratios. Regulatory developments include a revised enhanced leverage buffer rule, adopted early by the Firm; proposed stress-test transparency and SCB-volatility changes, plus 2026 scenarios and SCB levels through September 2027; and pending U.S. Basel III, GSIB surcharge, TLAC, and eligible long-term debt proposals. Their finalization and implementation remain uncertain, and the Firm is monitoring potential impacts.

nodes.title: Bank Capital and Stress-Test Regulatory Developments
key_items: Enhanced Transparency and Public Accountability of the Supervisory Stress Test
nodes.summary: The page notes Basel III SLR calculations for advanced-approaches banks, then covers regulatory developments: the 2025 eSLR final rule revises GSIB leverage buffers and related TLAC and eligible LTD requirements, effective April 2026, with JPMorganChase adopting early in January; proposed stress-test transparency and disclosure changes, alongside 2026 scenarios and unchanged SCBs through September 2027; a proposal to reduce SCB volatility by averaging two years of stress results and adjusting timing and reporting; and the U.S. Basel III proposal to replace the Advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach and apply the SCB to both that and the Standardized approach.

nodes.title: GSIB Surcharge and TLAC and Eligible LTD Requirements
GSIB Surcharge and TLAC and Eligible LTD Requirements (intro)
nodes.summary: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve proposed averaging quarterly GSIB surcharge calculations across each year, requiring daily averaging for some measures, reducing surcharge increments from 50 to 10 basis points, and making technical changes to Method 2—revising risk-based capital requirements for U.S. GSIBs. In August 2023, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC proposed extending eligible long-term debt and clean holding company requirements to banks with at least $100 billion in assets, limiting short-maturity debt counted toward GSIB TLAC, and expanding LTD capital deductions to covered non-GSIBs. Final rules and implementation dates remain uncertain; the Firm monitors developments and potential impacts.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s Basel III risk-based capital requirements: a 4.5% CET1 minimum plus buffers, including fixed or variable conservation buffers, GSIB surcharges, and a discretionary countercyclical buffer. The Firm’s 2025 and 2024 GSIB surcharges were 2.5% under Method 1 and 4.5% under Method 2; these remain unchanged for 2026. The countercyclical buffer was 0% at year-end 2025 and may rise to 2.5%. Falling below risk-based or leverage requirements restricts distributions and certain bonuses. It also describes TLAC and eligible debt requirements, early adoption of the eSLR rule effective January 1, 2026, the 3% SLR minimum plus a 2% buffer, and separate well-capitalized requirements for the Firm and its bank subsidiary, with further information cited in regulatory disclosures and notes.

nodes.title: TLAC and Supplementary Leverage Requirements
key_items: Leverage-based Capital Regulatory Requirements Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve requires U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, including JPMorgan Chase, to maintain minimum external TLAC and eligible long-term debt; the firm early adopted eSLR rule updates effective January 1, 2026. Advanced-approach organizations must meet a 3.0% minimum SLR, with the firm also subject to a 2.0% leverage buffer. SLR is Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure, based on average on-balance-sheet assets adjusted for permitted deductions plus specified off-balance-sheet exposures. Falling below the SLR requirement restricts capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, and certain executive bonuses. The text references further information on TLAC, SLR, and the eSLR rule.

nodes.title: Capital actions
key_items: Common stock dividends; Common stock repurchases
nodes.summary: The Firm’s capital actions include common dividends, share repurchases, and preferred stock. The Board declared a $1.50-per-share quarterly dividend payable January 31, 2026; dividends require quarterly Board approval, and payout ratios were 24% in 2025, 25% in 2024, and 29% in 2023. A new $50 billion repurchase authorization began July 1, 2025, following a prior $30 billion authorization. Repurchases totaled 114.4 million shares ($31.640 billion) in 2025, 91.7 million ($18.841 billion) in 2024, and 69.5 million ($9.898 billion) in 2023, excluding excise tax and commissions. Management controls timing and amounts based on market, regulatory, capital, and investment factors; repurchases have no price targets or timetable, may vary or be suspended, and can use open-market, private, or Rule 10b5-1 transactions. Further information is referenced in the filing. Preferred dividends were $1.1 billion, $1.3 billion, and $1.5 billion in 2025, 2024, and 2023; certain non-cumulative preferred series were issued and redeemed in 2025.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Management
Internal stress testing
nodes.summary: The text defines liquidity risk and outlines oversight by the independent Liquidity Risk Management function, including metrics, limits, breach processes, reviews, stress tests, and assumptions. Treasury and CIO manage liquidity to support client and financial obligations, optimize funding, comply with requirements, and maintain centralized liquidity across entities, while accounting for asset, liability, currency, and transfer restrictions. Governance involves firmwide and regional committees and Board Risk Committee review. Daily and event-driven stress tests model funding access, outflows, downgrades, collateral haircuts, and transfer constraints across scenarios, informing funding plans. Parent Company, IHC, and subsidiaries maintain liquidity to meet tolerances and requirements through stress.

nodes.title: Contingency funding plan
nodes.summary:
Contingency funding plan
The Firm’s Contingency Funding Plan (“CFP”) sets out the strategies for addressing and managing liquidity resource needs during a liquidity stress event and incorporates liquidity risk limits, indicators and risk appetite tolerances. The CFP also identifies the alternative contingent funding and liquidity resources available to the Firm and its legal entities in a period of stress.

nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.summary: The LCR rule requires the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to maintain eligible, unencumbered high-quality liquid assets (mainly cash and liquid securities) sufficient for 30 days of stressed net outflows, with a minimum LCR of 100%. Excess bank HQLA unavailable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA. The table reports average HQLA, outflows, LCRs, and excess HQLA for three quarters: the Firm’s December 2025 LCR was 111% versus 110% in September 2025 and 113% in December 2024; the bank’s was 115%, 117%, and 124%. Notes define eligible cash and securities, valuation, typical securities, and exclusions. The text explains drivers of year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter LCR declines for both entities, notes that LCRs fluctuate with business, Federal Reserve actions, and other factors, and directs readers to the Firm’s U.S. LCR disclosures for further liquidity-risk information.

nodes.title: Liquidity sources
nodes.summary: The Firm reported $548 billion of unencumbered marketable securities at year-end 2025, down from $594 billion in 2024, reflecting lower excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and fewer unencumbered Treasury and CIO investments; liquidity raised depends on market conditions. Available cash and securities totaled about $1.5 trillion versus $1.4 trillion, comprising eligible HQLA of $915 billion versus $834 billion and the securities above. FHLB and Federal Reserve discount-window borrowing capacity was $449 billion versus $413 billion, increased by additional pledged commercial loans, card receivables, and mortgages. This capacity excludes certain already-counted pledged assets and is not considered a primary liquidity source.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.summary: The NSFR measures whether large banking organizations have enough available stable funding to meet required funding needs over a one-year horizon. For the three months ended December 31, 2025, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. met the 100% minimum requirement, based on the Firm’s interpretation of the final rule. Further information is available in the Firm’s U.S. NSFR Disclosure report.

nodes.title: Funding
Funding Sources of funds

Funding comes from deposits, secured and unsecured capital-markets funding, and stockholders’ equity. Deposits are JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s primary funding source, supplemented by secured borrowings, unsecured long-term debt, or IHC borrowings. Non-bank subsidiaries rely mainly on long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowings, including securities lending and repurchase agreements. Excess funding is invested in securities or held in cash and other short-term liquid investments according to interest-rate and liquidity risks. Note 28 provides further information on off-balance-sheet obligations.

Average deposits rose in 2025 due to CIB and AWM growth, partly offset by lower CCB balances; year-end deposits rose across CIB, CCB, and AWM, with stated drivers and offsets. It provides estimated uninsured deposits and U.S. and non-U.S. uninsured time deposits by remaining maturity, deposit-to-liability and loans-to-deposit measures, and average deposit balances and interest rates by office, deposit type, and year for 2023–2025. nodes.title: Short-term funding
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s short- and long-term funding sources and trends. Short-term secured funding is mainly repos backed by high-quality securities; repo and other secured borrowing increased in 2025, largely from Markets financing needs. Unsecured short-term funding includes commercial paper and other borrowings; commercial paper fell due to liquidity management, while unsecured borrowing rose from structured-note issuance and fair-value changes. Long-term funding supports stable liquidity and is managed for diversification, market access, cost, client activity, and regulatory needs. The Parent issues most long-term debt and passes proceeds to the IHC. Tables report 2025 and 2024 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by instrument and issuer, and secured issuance and maturities for card securitizations, FHLB advances, and other secured funding. Tables report 2025 and 2024 unsecured issuance and maturities/redemptions by instrument and entity, noting certain Parent Company notes qualify as TLAC. nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.summary: Credit ratings affect the Firm’s financing access, cost, collateral and funding needs, investor and counterparty availability, and VIE and other commitments. The Firm considers downgrade impacts in liquidity risk and stress testing and believes it has sufficient liquidity to withstand reduced funding capacity. The text lists December 31, 2025 ratings and outlooks for the Parent Company and principal subsidiaries, and notes Moody’s 2025 outlook and rating changes. Unsecured debt has no downgrade-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits, or collateral requirements. Ratings depend on earnings diversity and stability, capital and liquidity, credit quality, risk controls, and funding diversity; agencies also assess economic, geopolitical, regulatory, profitability, risk, litigation, and methodological factors. See Notes 5 and 14 for related information.

Describes liquidity risk governance, centralized management, limits, monitoring, and daily and event-driven stress testing, along with the contingency funding plan and resources available under stress. Covers LCR and HQLA requirements, reported ratios and trends, and liquidity sources including securities, cash, and borrowing capacity; NSFR compliance; and funding adequacy, sources, balances, costs, issuance, maturities, and trends. Also explains how credit ratings affect funding and liquidity, lists ratings and changes, discusses downgrade resilience and rating factors, and points to related disclosures.

nodes.title: Reputation Risk Management
nodes.summary: Reputation risk is the potential harm to clients’, employees’ and investors’ trust, affinity or goodwill arising from the Firm’s decisions to engage or not engage with clients or business activities, potentially causing negative commercial impacts. Decisions weigh commercial factors such as capabilities, expertise, costs, risk and resource priorities, alongside reputation risk where relevant. The Firm manages this risk through policies, standards and procedures integrated across business lines and Corporate functions, with matters escalated to governance forums, including business-line committees, and regularly reported to the Board Risk Committee as appropriate.

Explains strategic and capital risk governance, assessment, planning, Board oversight, budget integration, capital strategy, stress testing and regulatory compliance. Covers capital rules and requirements, capital levels and changes, allocation and returns, distributions, and subsidiary requirements. Describes liquidity governance, limits, stress testing, contingency funding, liquidity and funding measures, resources, trends, and credit-rating impacts. Defines reputation risk and how it is considered in business decisions, managed through policies and procedures, escalated to governance forums, and reported to the Board Risk Committee.

nodes.title: Credit and Investment Risk Management
Credit Risk Management and Measurement
nodes.summary: Defines credit and investment risk and describes exposures across consumer, wholesale, investment, and cash activities. Credit Risk Management sets policies, procedures, limits, approval authorities, concentration guidelines, and monitors exposures, delinquencies, and estimated losses. Credit risk is measured using default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default, informing portfolio allowances and risk capital. Stress tests assess alternative economic, industry, and country scenarios, potential credit migration and losses, and guide risk appetite and counterparty decisions.

nodes.title: Stress testing
nodes.summary: Defines credit and investment risk as default or credit-profile deterioration, or investment principal/return loss. Describes exposures across consumer and wholesale lending, underwriting, trading, operations, securities financing, investment securities, and bank deposits. Credit Risk Management sets policies, limits, approvals, concentration guidelines, independently monitors troubled exposures and delinquencies, estimates losses, and supports capital management. Risk measurement uses default probability, loss severity, and exposure at default to estimate allowances and capital for potential unexpected losses. Stress tests apply centralized economic scenarios, assess portfolio and counterparty impacts, and inform risk appetite, supplemented by industry- and country-specific stresses.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and management
nodes.summary: The Firm’s credit-risk framework safeguards independent approvals through defined authorities, concentration limits, risk ratings, portfolio reviews, distressed-exposure guidance, and independent validation of models and assumptions. Consumer risks are monitored for delinquencies, trends, and concentrations against expectations, economic forecasts, and industry benchmarks, informing underwriting and loss estimates. Wholesale risks are reviewed at portfolio, industry, client, and counterparty levels, with periodically revised, stress-based limits. Mitigation includes underwriting, syndications, sales, securitizations, derivatives, netting, and collateral. Independent Credit Review assesses wholesale ratings, rating-change timeliness, and the effectiveness and policy compliance of credit management. Note 12 provides further loan details.

nodes.title: Risk reporting
nodes.summary: Credit Risk Management regularly reports aggregate exposures, credit quality forecasts, concentrations, and risk profile changes to senior leaders. Detailed portfolio reports cover industries, clients, counterparties, customers, products, and geography; senior management reviews the adequacy of credit-loss allowances at least quarterly. Risk trends and limit exceptions are shared with and discussed by risk committees, senior management, and the Board.

Consumer Credit Portfolio (intro)

nodes.title: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
Wholesale credit portfolio

nodes.title: Real Estate
nodes.summary: The 2025 Form 10-K details credit exposures and criticized-exposure trends for Real Estate and Consumer & Retail. Real Estate exposure was $224.9 billion, down from $207.1 billion in 2024; criticized exposure fell $714 million to $11.7 billion, as portfolio activity was largely offset by downgrades. Multifamily exposure is 99% performing and concentrated in California; overall exposure is 83% secured, with unsecured exposure largely investment-grade REITs and REOCs. Consumer & Retail exposure was $133.9 billion, up from $129.8 billion; criticized exposure rose $1.2 billion to $8.0 billion, driven by downgrades and new commitments, largely offset by portfolio activity. The tables compare 2025 and 2024 exposure by property or business category, including loans, commitments, derivatives, investment-grade shares, and drawn ratios. Notes define category coverage and explain collateralization and unsecured-credit quality.

nodes.title: Consumer & Retail
nodes.summary: Consumer & Retail credit exposure was $133.9 billion at year-end 2025; criticized exposure rose $1.2 billion to $8.0 billion, mainly from downgrades and new lending commitments, partly offset by portfolio activity. Tables compare 2025 and 2024 exposure by business and consumer services, retail, food and beverage, consumer hard goods, and leisure, including loans, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade share, and drawn share. Retail and leisure categories are defined; 88% of non-investment-grade leisure exposure is secured, and overall Consumer & Retail exposure is 57% secured, with 77% of unsecured exposure investment-grade. The text describes wholesale lending and refers to Note 12 for loan quality details. Nonaccrual loans rose $273 million in 2025 to $5.184 billion: downgrades in several industries were partly offset by charge-offs, upgrades, and sales in Healthcare and Consumer & Retail. A table details 2025 and 2024 nonaccrual activity. Wholesale net charge-offs rose to $1.598 billion from $822 million, with the rate increasing to 0.22% from 0.12%, driven by commercial and industrial losses, including technology, media and telecommunications and healthcare, and estimated borrower-fraud losses in secured facilities; the figures exclude noninterest-revenue gains or losses on nonaccrual-loan sales.

nodes.title: Wholesale Loans and Nonaccrual Activity
nodes.summary: The page describes wholesale lending to corporate, institutional, and high-net-worth clients and refers readers to Note 12 for loan credit-quality details. It reports nonaccrual loan activity for 2025 and 2024: exposure rose $273 million in 2025 to $5.184 billion, as sector downgrades were largely offset by charge-offs, upgrades, and sales elsewhere. It also explains that net charge-offs exclude noninterest-revenue gains or losses on nonaccrual loan sales and increased in 2025, mainly due to commercial and industrial losses and estimated borrower-fraud losses in secured lending.

nodes.title: Wholesale net charge-offs/(recoveries)
nodes.summary: Wholesale loan net charge-offs and recoveries for 2025 and 2024, in millions except ratios: average loans retained were $732,793 million and $673,310 million; gross charge-offs were $1,787 million and $1,022 million; gross recoveries collected were $189 million and $200 million; net charge-offs were $1,598 million and $822 million; and net charge-off rates were 0.22% and 0.12%, respectively.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: The text presents 2025 wholesale-loan maturities and fixed/variable rate distributions by loan class, with footnotes on resetting-rate loans and loans due within one year, and compares 2025 and 2024 net charge-offs/recoveries, average retained loans, and loss rates. It explains that contractual lending commitments overstate expected exposure because they are often unused or expire without default. It describes collateral, margin monitoring, and loss allowances for customer receivables. It also outlines derivatives’ risk-management uses and counterparty risks, netting and collateral protections, collateral-agreement coverage, derivative receivables of $57.8 billion in 2025 versus $61.0 billion in 2024, and additional collateral available to mitigate exposure.

nodes.title: Lending Commitments and Customer Receivables
nodes.summary: The Firm uses lending commitments and guarantees to meet client financing needs; their contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but generally do not reflect expected exposure or funding needs because they are usually not drawn, and are often refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expire without default. Customer receivables are collateralized brokerage margin loans. The Firm manages risk through margin requirements and ongoing monitoring, with collateral and margin calls generally mitigating losses so allowances are usually unnecessary; any required allowance reflects collateral value and default probability. Receivables appear in accrued interest and accounts receivable. See Notes 28 and 13 for further details.

nodes.title: Derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The text explains how JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives for client risk management, market-making and its own risk control, and describes counterparty and clearinghouse credit risks and mitigation through netting and collateral. It reports derivative receivables and collateral balances, ratings profiles for 2025 and 2024, and additional collateral held. It defines Peak, DRE and AVG exposure measures, explains CVA and wrong-way risk management, and notes that projected exposures generally decline after year one if no new trades are added.

nodes.title: Derivative Receivables and Credit Risk
nodes.summary: Tables show net derivative receivables after cash and other collateral for 2025 and 2024, and investment-grade versus noninvestment-grade exposure and shares. The Firm describes three collateral- and netting-aware credit-loss measures: Peak, used for limits and risk management; DRE, comparable to loan risk; and AVG, expected future fair value, used for pricing, capital, and CVA. CVA reflects counterparty credit quality and may be adjusted for wrong-way risk. Active risk management includes hedging with credit, interest-rate, foreign-exchange, equity, and commodity derivatives. A graph profiles Peak, DRE, and AVG exposure over ten years, generally declining after year one absent new trades.

nodes.title: Exposure profile of derivatives measures
nodes.summary: The text presents a chart of derivatives exposure profiles by maturity as of December 31, 2025, including average and peak measures. It explains that JPMorgan Chase uses credit derivatives as a market-maker and to manage its own credit risk. Credit portfolio management derivatives mitigate risk from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale derivatives counterparties; other end-user hedges, including certain market-making securities, are excluded. Net protection purchased and sold for credit portfolio management totaled $23.898 billion in 2025, versus $40.888 billion in 2024. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are marked to fair value through principal transactions revenue, while related loans and commitments use accrual accounting, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall exposure-value changes. CDS hedge effectiveness can differ because of reference entities, contractual credit-event definitions, and maturities; the Firm generally aligns protection and exposure maturities and monitors and manages differences. Further details are in Note 5.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.summary:

Credit derivatives
The Firm uses credit derivatives for two primary purposes: first, in its capacity as a market-maker, and second, as an end-user to manage the Firm’s own credit risk associated with various exposures.

nodes.title: Credit portfolio management activities
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives to manage credit risk on loans, lending commitments and wholesale-business derivative counterparty exposures; other derivatives used to manage risks such as market-making securities are excluded. Net protection purchased or sold for credit portfolio management was $23.9 billion in 2025, versus $40.9 billion in 2024, covering loans and related commitments and derivative receivables. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are marked to fair value through principal transactions revenue, while managed loans are accrued, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall exposure-value changes. Hedge effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, contract terms and maturities; the Firm generally matches protection and exposure maturities and monitors and manages differences.

The section reviews wholesale credit risk sources, portfolio composition, growth and active management, including loan, commitment, acquired-asset, collateral, protection and nonperforming exposures. It presents maturity, internal-rating and industry profiles, defines investment-grade and criticized classifications, and details real estate and Consumer & Retail exposures, collateral, concentrations and trends. It covers wholesale lending, nonaccrual activity, charge-offs and maturities; explains commitments and customer receivables; and describes derivative counterparty risk, netting, collateral, exposure measures, CVA, credit derivatives, portfolio hedging, accounting treatment and related earnings volatility.

Allocation of allowance for loan losses

It describes increased emphasis on adverse macroeconomic scenarios, unemployment and GDP forecasts, and future estimate updates, with references to related disclosures. Detailed 2025–2024 tables show allowance rollforwards, charge-offs, recoveries, provisions, impairment methods, loan balances, credit ratios and rates, plus allowance allocation by loan class and footnotes on receivables, nonaccrual policy and the Apple Card transaction.

nodes.title: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
nodes.summary: Investment portfolio risk covers potential principal losses or reduced returns on long-term securities and principal investments. Treasury and CIO held $774.0 billion in investment securities at year-end 2025, averaging AA+, with default risk mitigated by high credit quality; governance includes risk committees, independent valuation review, and approved limits. Principal investments—such as tax-oriented, private equity, debt, and real-asset holdings—totaled $47.0 billion, up from $42.4 billion in 2024; oversight includes independent approvals, portfolio limits, valuation review, and stress testing. Market risk management defines policies, measures and monitors exposure using VaR, stress tests, drawdowns, earnings and economic-value sensitivities, and other metrics. Limits reflect market and business factors, are reviewed and approved, and breaches are reported, escalated, and addressed. Risk models have limitations and are periodically reviewed and calibrated.

Describes credit and investment risk exposures, governance, measurement, stress testing, monitoring, mitigation, and reporting. Covers firmwide, consumer, and wholesale portfolios—including loans, commitments, counterparties, derivatives, securities, concentrations, credit quality, delinquencies, nonperforming exposures, charge-offs, and related controls and disclosures. Summarizes allowance-for-credit-loss methods, balances, drivers, and historical tables. Also reviews investment securities and principal investments, their exposures and oversight, and market-risk metrics, limits, model limitations, and escalation processes.

nodes.title: Market Risk Management
Market Risk Management and Measurement
key_items: Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.summary: Market risk arises when market factors—including interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatility—change asset and liability values. Market Risk Management sets firmwide policies and procedures, measures and monitors risk independently, defines and oversees limits, conducts stress tests and qualitative assessments, and supports efficient risk-return decisions, reduced operating-performance volatility, and transparency for management, directors, and regulators. It uses multiple statistical and nonstatistical measures: value-at-risk, stress testing, profit-and-loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, economic-value sensitivity, and other sensitivity measures.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and control
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s market-risk controls: limits are tailored to market conditions and business strategy, measured at firm, business, and legal-entity levels, reviewed and approved by management, monitored for compliance, and escalated or remedied when breached. It notes model limitations and ongoing measure improvements. A table maps CCB, CIB, AWM, and Corporate activities to their market risks, positions measured by VaR, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity measures. It then describes Risk Management and Regulatory VaR frameworks, assumptions, uses, aggregation, data and proxy limitations, model updates, and their differing horizons, confidence levels, covered positions, diversification treatment, and regulatory-capital role.

nodes.title: VaR
Value-at-risk
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes its historical-simulation VaR framework, using 12 months of data, daily granular portfolio models, and aggregation to measure and report market risk. Risk Management VaR uses a one-day horizon and approximately 95% confidence; Regulatory VaR uses a ten-day horizon and approximately 99%, applies to Basel III covered positions, and differs in scope and diversification treatment. The text explains VaR’s data, liquidity, and forecasting limitations; use of proxies, stress tests, valuation data, and periodic model enhancements; and references to valuation, model-risk, and regulatory disclosures. It presents 2025 and 2024 VaR averages, minima, maxima, components, and diversification benefits, with notes on included exposures and unusual positions. A 2025 proxy refinement would have lowered reported average VaR, and average Total VaR fell $7 million year over year, mainly from reduced Visa exposure and market volatility rolling out, partly offset by higher commodities and equities risk.

nodes.title: Total VaR

Average total VaR fell $7 million in 2025 versus 2024, mainly from lower Visa exposure and foreign-exchange and fixed-income volatility, partly offset by higher commodities and equities exposure; a graph shows daily VaR over four quarters.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. Dollar FX Risk
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk arises when exchange-rate changes affect the Firm’s assets, liabilities, or future results. Structural exposures stem from capital investments, forecasted expenses and revenues, investment securities, and foreign-currency debt. Treasury and CIO, in partnership with the LOBs, primarily manage these risks and may hedge some with derivatives; further information is referenced on page 63.

Explains how JPMorganChase identifies, measures, monitors, and controls market risk from changes in rates, currencies, prices, spreads, and volatility. Covers firmwide risk governance, limits, escalation, model limitations, and the Risk Management and Regulatory VaR frameworks; VaR results, drivers, backtesting, stress testing, and drawdowns; earnings-at-risk and economic-value sensitivity, including structural interest-rate risk and Treasury/CIO hedging; non-U.S. dollar foreign-exchange exposures; other sensitivity measures; and country-risk measurement, controls, assumptions, and reporting differences.

nodes.title: Country Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text describes the Firm’s independent country-risk function, which sets policies and sovereign ratings, monitors exposures and limits, develops early-warning tools, and provides stress analysis. It explains how country exposure is attributed and measured across deposits, lending, securities, derivatives, and other activities, noting exclusions, assumptions, and differences from FFIEC reporting. It outlines tailored crisis stress testing and regular reporting, then presents 2025 and comparative 2024 top-20 non-U.S. country exposures, measurement notes, UK exposure growth, and Russia exposure and litigation disclosures.

nodes.title: Climate Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text outlines climate risk as physical (acute, chronic and indirect impacts) and transition risk from the shift to a lower-carbon economy, and describes firmwide climate-risk responsibilities, business-unit duties and Board and committee oversight. It then defines operational risk and its framework, governance and accountability; explains business self-assessments, independent oversight, quantitative measurement using loss models and capital methods, stress testing and treatment of insurance; and notes that independent control testing and monitoring are integral to the framework.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Management
Operational Risk Management Framework
key_items: Operational Risk Governance; Operational Risk Identification; Operational Risk Measurement
Management of Operational Risk; Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.summary: Operational risk encompasses losses from failed processes, systems, people, or external events, including compliance, conduct, legal, and model risk. The Firm’s CCOR framework governs identification, measurement, monitoring, testing, remediation, and reporting, with responsibilities shared among business units, control managers, independent CCOR officers, and Board oversight. Risk is identified through self-assessments and independent reviews; measured through control assessments, loss modeling, capital estimates, and stress testing; and monitored through independent control testing. Findings prompt remediation plans and escalation, while standardized reporting tracks indicators, risk appetite, and matters requiring senior management or Board attention.
