nodes.summary: The text outlines operational-risk categories—compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risk—and describes firmwide resiliency, payment fraud, and third-party outsourcing risks and controls. It defines cybersecurity risk, explaining evolving threats, protections, third-party and client exposures, and potential impacts. It details the Information Security Program, its leadership and functions (cyber operations, technology governance, awareness, and resiliency), incident response and external collaboration, plus governance and oversight by management committees, independent risk management, external assessors, and the Board and its Audit and Risk Committees.

nodes.title: Compliance Risk Management
nodes.summary: Compliance risk is the risk of failing to meet applicable laws, regulations, rules, conduct codes, or self-regulatory standards. Business lines and Corporate own and manage this risk, while the independent Operational Risk and Compliance organization oversees, monitors, tests, and reports on it through policies and standards. Risks span jurisdictions, products, customer relationships, employee activity, anti-money laundering, trading, market conduct, cross-border services, and fiduciary duties; other functions oversee obligations in their areas. The Global CCO and risk executive lead the function, coordinate oversight through the CCOR Management Framework, and update Board committees on significant issues. The Code of Conduct sets integrity expectations, requires reporting violations and unethical conduct, provides periodic training and annual affirmations, and enables anonymous global hotline reports with translation services. It prohibits retaliation, and the Audit Committee periodically receives program reports.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk Management
nodes.summary: Conduct risk is an operational risk arising from employee actions or misconduct that may cause unfair customer outcomes, undermine market integrity, harm employees or the Firm, or damage its reputation. Each line of business and Corporate is responsible for managing this risk and sustaining a culture guided by the Firm’s Business Principles and Code, which explains employee conduct expectations and ethical, legal compliance resources. Oversight is coordinated like compliance risk. Management spans the employee life cycle, and business units, Treasury and CIO, and designated corporate functions periodically assess risk, review relevant metrics and issues, and provide conduct education as appropriate.

nodes.title: Legal Risk Management
nodes.summary: Legal risk is operational risk arising from actual or alleged failure to meet legal obligations under applicable law, agreements, and the Firm’s products and services. The global Legal function manages litigation, enforcement, reviews and investigations; advises on products, contracts, disclosures, marketing, new initiatives, laws, regulation, advocacy, and Firm matters; resolves disputes; manages outside counsel; and advises the Conflicts Office on potentially conflicting wholesale transactions. The General Counsel reports to the CEO, serves on key Firm committees, and, with other Legal leaders, reports significant matters to the Board and Audit Committee. Legal also advises committees, business lines, and Corporate on potential reputational risks.

nodes.title: Estimations and Model Risk Management
nodes.summary: Estimation and model risk is operational risk arising when decisions rely on incorrect or misused outputs. The Firm uses models, including AI and machine learning, for valuation, risk, capital, stress testing, credit-loss allowances and business decisions. Independent MRGR governs relevant policies, tiers models by complexity, exposure and reliance, and reviews methodology, assumptions and testing. Business users and developers own, develop, test, maintain and monitor models, and refer new or materially changed models for approval before use. Exceptions may permit interim use with risk mitigations. Uncertainty can rise when market or economic conditions differ from historical data or acquired assets differ from model inputs, requiring greater judgment. The text also refers readers to accounting-estimate and valuation disclosures.

Describes the Firm’s operational-risk framework, including shared governance, risk identification, measurement, monitoring, testing, remediation, reporting, and insurance. Covers compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risks, alongside resiliency, payment fraud, outsourcing, and cybersecurity threats and controls. Explains relevant responsibilities, policies, oversight, employee conduct standards and reporting channels, Legal’s advisory and dispute functions, and independent model governance, review, approval, and management of uncertainty.

Allowance for credit losses
key_items: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes controls and governance for complex accounting estimates, emphasizing consistent methods, independent review, and appropriate carrying values. Its credit-loss allowance covers loans, lending commitments, and investment securities, requiring judgment about forecasts, historical losses, risks, ratings, collateral, and asset life. Estimates use an eight-quarter forecast with portfolio-specific economic variables; scenario comparisons show modeled loss sensitivities, while limitations include nonlinear effects, scenario weighting, and changing portfolios or behavior. The Firm also notes Apple Card allowance assumptions, excludes that portfolio from sensitivity analysis during model integration, and considers its 2025 estimates reasonable.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase measures some assets and liabilities at fair value, mainly on a recurring basis (including trading positions, AFS securities, structured notes and securities financing agreements), and certain loans on a nonrecurring basis using collateral values. The table reports fair-value assets by category, Level 3 amounts and ratios to Firm assets; derivative-receivable Level 3 figures exclude netting. Valuation requires judgment, especially for Level 3 instruments with significant unobservable inputs, and depends on models, market data, adjustments for credit, funding and liquidity, and market conditions. Estimation uncertainty and differing methods or assumptions can change reported values; Note 2 details the processes and hierarchy.

nodes.title: Goodwill impairment
nodes.summary: Under U.S. GAAP, goodwill is allocated to reporting units and tested for impairment at least annually; the Firm’s methodology is described in Note 15, and testing involves significant management judgment. For 2025, management considered economic conditions, estimated market cost of equity, actual results, and performance projections, concluding goodwill was not impaired at December 31. Each reporting unit’s fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 20%, with no significant impairment risk indicated. Projections reflect short-term business outlook and long-term growth and return-on-equity estimates, benchmarked against third-party and peer data where possible. Note 15 provides further details.

nodes.title: Credit card rewards liability
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase rewards credit cardholders with points based on account activity; points generally have no earning limits or expiration and can be redeemed for cash or account credits, gift cards, and travel. The Firm accrues an estimated liability as points are earned and reduces it upon redemption. The liability, recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities, rose from $14.4 billion in 2024 to $16.0 billion in 2025, as points earned through higher spending and promotions outpaced redemptions. It depends on redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions, reviewed periodically using historical results, customer behavior, and management judgment. A combined 25-basis-point increase in redemption rate and 1-basis-point increase in cost per point would raise the 2025 liability by about $512 million.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase explains that income tax accounting across its U.S. and international jurisdictions requires judgments about complex laws, transactions, taxable-income timing, and uncertain positions, which may be challenged by tax authorities and resolved through audits, appeals, or courts. Estimates and unrecognized tax benefits are reviewed and updated as laws, interpretations, strategies, and information change; revisions may materially affect results or the effective tax rate. Deferred taxes arise from book-tax differences and are measured at enacted rates; deferred tax assets, including NOL, foreign tax credit, and business credit carryforwards, are assessed for likely realization using future-income estimates and tax-planning strategies, with valuation allowances established or reversed as appropriate. As of December 31, 2025, management judged deferred tax assets realizable net of the allowance. Current and deferred provisions rely on estimates that may differ from filed returns; resulting adjustments are generally recorded when returns are filed and global tax effects are known. See Note 25.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of income
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated income statements for 2023–2025, including revenue components, interest income and expense, credit-loss provisions, operating expenses, pretax income, taxes, net income, common earnings per share, and weighted-average shares. Also reports consolidated comprehensive income for those years, detailing after-tax other comprehensive gains and losses from investment securities, currency translation, fair value and cash flow hedges, benefit plans, and fair-value-option liabilities. Notes are integral to both statements.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of comprehensive income
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated comprehensive income for 2023–2025, including net income, after-tax other comprehensive income or loss by category, and comprehensive income. Provides balance sheets for 2024 and 2025 detailing assets, liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and stockholders’ equity, with related fair-value, pledged-asset, allowance, and share information. Also summarizes assets and liabilities of consolidated variable interest entities (VIEs), noting their use to settle VIE obligations and the generally limited recourse of beneficial-interest holders. Financial-statement notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.summary: Presents JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated balance sheets for 2025 and 2024, listing assets, liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and stockholders’ equity, with fair-value and pledged-asset details. An accompanying table summarizes consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and explains their settlement and limited recourse. The text also reports 2023–2025 changes in stockholders’ equity, including preferred and common stock, paid-in capital, earnings, dividends, comprehensive income or loss, and treasury-stock activity, and notes accounting-guidance adoptions.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2023–2025 consolidated statements of changes in stockholders’ equity and cash flows. Equity details cover preferred and common stock, paid-in capital, retained earnings, dividends, comprehensive income or loss, treasury stock activity, and total equity, with notes on accounting guidance adopted in 2023 and 2024. Cash flows classify operating, investing, and financing activity, report exchange-rate effects and changes in cash balances, and disclose cash interest and taxes paid. The financial-statement notes are integral to both statements.

nodes.title: Consolidated statements of cash flows
key_items: Net cash provided by/(used in) financing activities
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s consolidated cash flow statement presents 2025, 2024, and 2023 figures (in millions). It details operating cash flows, including net income and adjustments; investing cash flows, including securities, loans, and the First Republic acquisition; and financing cash flows, including deposits, borrowings, stock transactions, and dividends. It also reports exchange-rate effects, changes in cash balances, beginning and ending cash, and cash interest and income taxes paid. The accompanying notes are integral to the statements.

Presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2023–2025 consolidated income, comprehensive income, changes in stockholders’ equity, and cash flows, plus 2024–2025 balance sheets. Coverage includes revenues, expenses, earnings, taxes, other comprehensive gains and losses, equity and treasury-stock activity, operating, investing and financing cash flows, cash balances, and cash interest and taxes paid. It also summarizes consolidated VIE assets and liabilities, related fair-value and pledged-asset information, accounting-guidance adoptions, and an independent auditor’s procedures for Level 3 fair-value estimates. Notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
Note 1 - Basis of presentation
Consolidation
nodes.summary: Note 1 describes JPMorganChase’s business, U.S. GAAP and regulatory accounting basis, and consolidation policies. It explains consolidation of controlled voting-interest entities and VIEs, equity-method and fair-value accounting for significant-influence investments and investment funds, VIE/SPE characteristics, primary-beneficiary tests, and ongoing reassessment. It also covers interest and customer-contract revenue recognition, fair-value gains and losses, management estimates, foreign-currency translation and transaction effects, and permitted net presentation of specified derivatives, collateral, and securities-financing balances under enforceable master netting agreements.

nodes.title: VIE Consolidation and Financial Reporting Policies
key_items: Interest income; Revenue from contracts with customers; Principal transactions revenue
Use of estimates in the preparation of consolidated financial statements; Foreign currency translation
Use of estimates in the preparation of consolidated financial statements
nodes.summary: Explains how the Firm assesses power and economic exposure when deciding whether to consolidate VIEs, including ongoing reassessments. Covers interest income recognition, customer-contract revenue and fair-value changes reported mainly in principal transactions revenue. Notes that financial statements rely on estimates that may differ from actual results, and describes foreign-currency revaluation and where translation and transaction gains or losses are reported.

nodes.title: Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP permits net presentation of certain derivatives, collateral, and securities-financing balances when enforceable master netting agreements and other conditions apply; the Firm elects this treatment where eligible. Such agreements enable termination, valuation, net settlement, and collateral/margin transfer or liquidation upon default. Related details are referenced in Notes 5 and 11. Cash-flow statements define cash as cash and due from banks plus deposits with banks. A 2024 tax-credit accounting adoption changed amortization classification, reduced retained earnings $161 million, and raised first-quarter tax expense and effective tax rate without materially affecting net income. 2023 adoptions covered portfolio-layer fair-value hedging, with immaterial retained-earnings impact, and troubled-debt-restructuring guidance, increasing retained earnings $446 million.

nodes.title: Netting, Cash Flows, and New Accounting Guidance
nodes.summary: Describes how master netting agreements terminate and net derivative, repurchase, and securities-lending transactions after default, including collateral requirements, set-off, and liquidation rights; refers readers to Notes 5 and 11. Defines cash in the consolidated cash flow statements as cash and due from banks and deposits with banks. Summarizes 2024 adoption of proportional amortization for eligible tax-credit investments: modified retrospective adoption reclassified certain alternative-energy investment amortization from other income to income tax expense, reduced retained earnings by $161 million, and raised first-quarter tax expense and the effective tax rate by about $450 million and two percentage points, with no material net-income impact.

nodes.title: Accounting standards adopted January 1, 2023
key_items: Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method
Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings (“TDRs”)
nodes.summary: Effective January 1, 2023, the Firm adopted guidance expanding portfolio-layer fair value hedging, transferring HTM securities to AFS and designating them in a hedge; the retained-earnings impact was immaterial. It also adopted revised TDR credit-loss guidance, electing a non-DCF portfolio approach for most modified loans to troubled borrowers while retaining DCF for collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans. Modified-retrospective adoption increased retained earnings by $446 million.

nodes.title: Significant accounting policies
nodes.summary: The section lists JPMorganChase’s significant accounting policies and points to the notes and pages with detailed descriptions: fair value measurement and option; derivatives; revenue and expenses; employee benefits and incentives; securities and securities financing; loans and credit-loss allowances; variable-interest entities; goodwill and other intangible assets; premises, equipment, and leases; liabilities and debt; earnings per share; income taxes; off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees; and litigation.

Note 1 outlines JPMorganChase’s business, U.S. GAAP and regulatory accounting basis, consolidation policies for controlled entities and VIEs, significant-influence investments and investment funds, and ongoing VIE assessment. It describes interest and customer-contract revenue recognition, fair-value changes, estimates, foreign-currency accounting, eligible netting under enforceable agreements, and the cash-flow definition of cash. It summarizes 2024 tax-credit and 2023 hedge-accounting and credit-loss-guidance adoptions and their effects, and lists significant accounting policies with references to detailed disclosures.

nodes.title: Note 2 - Fair value measurement
Valuation process
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase explains recurring and nonrecurring fair value measurement, defining fair value and describing use of market prices, valuation models, observable and unobservable inputs, adjustments, and management judgment. Risk functions estimate values; the independent Valuation Control Group verifies them and sets adjustments, under oversight by the Valuation Governance Forum. Verification uses independent data and additional reviews for less observable prices or complex positions. Adjustments may address liquidity, large net open risk positions, uncertainty in unobservable inputs, counterparty credit (CVA), own credit (DVA), and funding (FVA); Level 1 quoted prices are not adjusted.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.summary: When market prices or comparable quotes are unavailable, fair value is generally estimated using models based on transaction terms and market-based or independently sourced inputs, which are subject to the described price-verification process. MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before implementation under Firm policy. Exceptions may permit interim use before approval, potentially subject to risk-mitigation measures such as trading limits.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: Explains the U.S. GAAP three-level fair value hierarchy, based on input observability, and classification by the lowest significant input level. It outlines JPMorgan’s valuation methods and typical hierarchy classifications for securities financing, wholesale and consumer loans, securities, commodities, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, private equity, fund investments, VIE beneficial interests, and structured notes. Methods include market quotes, broker data, discounted cash flows, models, NAV, and adjustments for credit, funding, liquidity, and instrument-specific risks. It introduces tables of assets and liabilities measured at fair value in 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: The text presents JPMorgan Chase’s recurring fair-value assets and liabilities for 2025 and 2024, broken down by fair-value hierarchy levels 1–3 and derivative netting adjustments, across trading assets, available-for-sale securities, loans, servicing rights, other assets, and liabilities. Footnotes explain GSE mortgage-related obligations, a 2025 hierarchy reclassification, commodity inventory valuation, long/short securities offsets, investments using NAV practical expedients, and derivative netting. It also describes Level 3 valuation governance, models, significant unobservable inputs and their reported ranges and averages, and cautions that these statistics reflect instrument characteristics rather than input uncertainty or estimate reasonableness.

nodes.title: Fair value measurements using significant unobservable inputs
Level 3 valuations
nodes.summary: The Firm describes its processes for valuing Level 3 instruments, noting that fair-value estimates require greater judgment because significant inputs are unobservable. Management selects appropriate models and derives inputs from relevant empirical data, such as transactions, rates, curves, prepayment and default assumptions, volatilities, correlations, prices, comparable valuations, foreign exchange rates, and credit curves. A referenced table reports primary Level 3 instruments, techniques, significant unobservable inputs, ranges, and averages; it excludes observable Level 1 and 2 components, whose risks are managed with Level 1 or 2 positions. Input ranges show highest and lowest values, while weighted averages are based on instrument fair values. These statistics describe portfolio characteristics and distributions, not uncertainty or estimate reasonableness, and vary with instruments’ features and holdings over time.

nodes.title: Level 3 inputs (a)
nodes.summary: The table reports JPMorgan Chase’s December 31, 2025 Level 3 fair-value assets and liabilities, valuation techniques, and significant unobservable inputs, including ranges and averages. It covers mortgage-backed securities and loans, corporate and government debt, interest-rate, credit, foreign-exchange, equity and commodity derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, borrowings, deposits, and other items. Notes explain category aggregation, instrument composition, structured-note valuation, equity securities valued internally, price inputs, forward-equity-price units, and averaging methods.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.summary: The text explains how changes in unobservable valuation inputs affect fair value, noting that inputs may interact, inverse relationships generally apply, and links between observable and unobservable inputs are excluded. It defines yield, credit spread, prepayment speed, conditional default rate, loss severity, correlation, volatility, Bermudan swaption switch value, interest rate curves, and forward prices; describes relevant instrument, collateral, market, and contract factors shaping their ranges; and states each input’s typical valuation impact, including cases where direction depends on position or conditions.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.summary: Presents 2023–2025 rollforwards of Level 3 recurring fair-value assets and liabilities by financial-instrument category, showing opening and closing values, gains and losses, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and transfers. Explains that Level 3 classifications reflect significant unobservable inputs but also include observable valuation components; results exclude related Level 1 and 2 risk-management positions. Notes Level 3 shares of fair-valued assets and liabilities, net presentation of derivatives, income-statement/OCI treatment of gains and losses, immaterial AFS and realized DVA amounts, unrealized DVA figures, and definitions of purchases and settlements.

nodes.title: Level 3 analysis
key_items: Consolidated balance sheets changes; For the year ended December 31, 2025
nodes.summary: The text reports recurring fair-value Level 3 asset changes: assets totaled $25.1 billion at December 31, 2025, up $1.3 billion from 2024. The increase mainly reflected $474 million in gross derivative receivables from gains and purchases, largely offset by settlements and net transfers, and $646 million in non-trading loans from purchases and net transfers, largely offset by settlements. Nonrecurring-basis changes are discussed elsewhere.

nodes.title: Transfers between levels for instruments carried at fair value on a recurring basis
nodes.summary: The text reports significant recurring fair-value transfers between Levels 2 and 3 for 2023–2025, by instrument and amount, attributing them mainly to changes in input observability and the significance of unobservable inputs; transfers are assumed at the start of the quarter. It summarizes annual gains on assets and losses on liabilities for 2023–2025, driven chiefly by derivative and long-term-debt market movements and, in 2023–2024, mortgage-servicing-right gains. It also explains derivative CVA and FVA methods and inputs, presents related principal-transactions results for 2023–2025, and describes DVA accounting for fair-value-option liabilities, including recognition in revenue or OCI.

Describes Level 3 fair-value valuation methods, significant unobservable inputs, reported ranges and weighted averages, and their limitations and valuation effects. Covers instruments and input definitions, factors influencing inputs, and 2023–2025 rollforwards, portfolio analysis, and transfers between Levels 2 and 3. Reports changes in Level 3 assets, related gains and losses, purchases, sales, issuances and settlements, and explains treatment of observable components, risk-management positions, derivative CVA/FVA, and debt valuation adjustments in earnings or OCI.

nodes.title: Credit & funding adjustments & Assets and liabilities measured at FV on a nonrecurring basis
key_items: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.summary: Derivative fair values use observable-market models but are adjusted for counterparty credit risk (CVA) and, when market participants would include it, funding costs (FVA). CVA uses expected positive exposure, default probabilities from CDS spreads, recovery estimates, and contractual mitigants such as collateral and offset rights. FVA for uncollateralized or partially collateralized OTC derivatives considers expected funding needs and market funding costs, including the Firm’s credit risk for liabilities; collateralized derivatives use OIS discounting and need no separate FVA. The text reports annual CVA and FVA gains or losses for 2023–2025, excluding hedges, and explains that FVA includes own-credit effects. For fair-value-option liabilities, DVA reflects post-issuance changes in default probability and loss given default estimated from bond spreads; realized gains or losses enter principal transactions revenue, while unrealized amounts enter OCI.

nodes.title: Assets and Liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.summary: Presents nonrecurring fair-value measurements for assets and liabilities held at December 31, 2025 and 2024, by product category and fair-value hierarchy level, including loans, other assets, and accounts payable and other liabilities. Notes that 2025 Level 3 other assets include equity securities valued using the measurement alternative and impairments of equity-method investments. Reports nonrecurring fair-value gains and losses for 2025, 2024, and 2023 by category and in total, including measurement-alternative results and equity-method investment impairments.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.summary: The text explains the measurement alternative for equity securities without readily determinable fair values: cost less impairment, adjusted for observable prices of identical or similar issuer investments, with changes recognized in other income and valuation adjustments applied where appropriate. It reports 2025/2024 carrying values of $4.873/$3.737 billion, upward changes of $224/$89 million and downward changes or impairment of $102/$286 million, plus cumulative changes since 2018. It describes restricted Visa B-2 shares, uncertain litigation and conversion terms, Visa’s announced exchange offer, and related fair-valued derivatives. It then outlines required fair-value disclosures for financial instruments not carried at fair value, lists instruments whose carrying values approximate fair value, and presents 2025/2024 carrying and estimated fair values by hierarchy level for financial assets and liabilities. Loan valuation methods, reasons fair and carrying values differ, and an exclusion of lending commitments are noted.

nodes.title: Estimated FV of financial instruments & Trading assets and liabilities
key_items: Financial instruments for which carrying value approximates fair value
nodes.summary: The notes disclose estimated fair values and hierarchy classifications for financial assets and liabilities not measured at fair value on a recurring basis at December 31, 2025 and 2024, while noting excluded assets and relationships add significant value. Short-term, low-credit-risk instruments generally approximate carrying value; GAAP requires demand, savings, and certain money-market deposits to equal carrying value, without recognizing their funding value. Loan valuation methods and reasons for fair-value differences are explained. Wholesale lending-related commitments’ carrying and estimated fair values are presented, with exclusions noted; consumer off-balance-sheet commitments are not valued because they may often be reduced or canceled.

Explains JPMorganChase’s fair-value policies, governance, model approval, valuation techniques, adjustments, and U.S. GAAP hierarchy. Presents recurring and nonrecurring fair-value assets and liabilities for 2025 and 2024, including Level 3 inputs, rollforwards, transfers, gains and losses, and disclosures on CVA, FVA, and DVA. Covers equity securities valued using the measurement alternative, Visa-related holdings and derivatives, and estimated fair values and hierarchy classifications for financial instruments not carried at fair value, including loans and lending commitments.

nodes.title: Note 3 - Fair value option
Note 3 - Fair value option (intro)
nodes.summary: The fair value option allows election of fair value for selected financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments. The Firm uses it to reduce income-statement volatility from differing measurement bases and to reflect instruments managed on a fair value basis. Elections cover certain loans and lending commitments, securities financing agreements, securitized-asset interests with embedded credit derivatives, client-driven structured notes and other hybrid instruments, and certain long-term interests issued by CIB consolidated securitization trusts whose underlying assets are carried at fair value.

nodes.title: Changes in fair value under the fair value option election
nodes.summary: The text reports 2025–2023 income-statement fair-value changes for instruments elected under the fair value option, excluding related risk-management instruments, and explains presentation of credit-risk gains/losses, classifications, excluded contractual interest, and structured-note risk management. It describes how instrument-specific credit risk is measured for loans and commitments, long-term debt, and securities-financing agreements. Tables compare contractual principal and fair value for elected loans, long-term debt, and beneficial interests at year-end 2025 and 2024, with explanatory definitions and exclusions. It also gives elected lending-commitment amounts and fair values for both years.

nodes.title: Structured note products by balance sheet classification and risk component
nodes.summary: The table reports fair values of structured notes by balance-sheet classification—long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and deposits—and primary risk exposure (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, and commodity) at December 31, 2025 and 2024. Total structured notes were $164.965 billion in 2025 and $143.804 billion in 2024. A note excludes deposits linked to precious metals for which the fair value option was not elected: $2.8 billion and $869 million, respectively.

Explains why the Firm elects fair value for selected assets, liabilities, commitments, and hybrid instruments, including to reduce measurement-related earnings volatility and reflect fair-value management. Reports 2025–2023 fair-value changes, presentation and measurement of instrument-specific credit risk, excluded interest, and risk management; compares contractual principal with fair value for elected loans, debt, beneficial interests, and lending commitments in 2025 and 2024. Also presents structured-note fair values by balance-sheet classification and risk exposure for both years, with an exclusion for certain precious-metal-linked deposits.

nodes.title: Note 4 - Credit risk concentrations
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes how it monitors and manages credit-risk concentrations: consumer exposures by product and U.S. region, and wholesale exposures by industry and counterparty, with senior oversight, underwriting adjustments, collateral, and risk-transfer tools. It reports on- and off-balance-sheet consumer and wholesale credit exposures for 2025 and 2024 across consumer categories and wholesale industries, including loans, derivatives, and lending-related instruments. Notes explain classifications, exclusions, collateralized brokerage receivables, government securities, other exposures, and the estimated Apple Card portfolio commitment.

nodes.title: Note 5 - Derivative instruments
Derivative Instruments, Risk Management and Clearing
nodes.summary: The page describes derivatives’ value and uses: market-making for clients and managing or hedging the Firm’s risks. Client exposures are offset with derivatives or other instruments. Risk management derivatives address interest-rate, foreign-exchange, commodity-inventory and counterparty credit risks, with gains and losses expected to offset related variability; credit derivatives, primarily CDS, pay upon specified credit events. Contracts include bilateral OTC, exchange-traded and OTC-cleared derivatives involving CCPs. The Firm also clears client derivatives but does not report those contracts in its consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Accounting for derivatives
Accounting for derivatives (intro)
nodes.summary: The Firm records all freestanding derivatives executed for its own account on the consolidated balance sheets at fair value. Under U.S. GAAP, derivative assets and liabilities and related cash collateral may be offset when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists. Accounting for changes in derivative value depends on hedge-accounting designation and qualification; derivatives not designated as hedges are measured at fair value through earnings. Related tables disclose derivative amounts and reporting of assets, liabilities, gains and losses, while Notes 1–3 provide further discussion of offsetting and embedded derivatives in structured notes.

nodes.title: Derivatives designated as hedges
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase applies hedge accounting to selected risk-management derivatives, subject to documented objectives and quarterly effectiveness assessments; accounting is discontinued when a hedge is not highly effective. The text explains fair value, cash flow, and net investment hedge treatment, including earnings, OCI/AOCI, basis adjustments, termination, and portfolio-layer accounting. A table maps derivative types and uses to hedge designations or disclosure categories, including identified exposures, mortgage and lending risks, market-making and other activities, and affected business segments and page references.

nodes.title: Notional amount of derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s derivative notional amounts by contract type for 2025 and 2024, totaling $50.642 billion and $47.723 billion, respectively, and explains that notionals indicate activity rather than likely losses because they generally serve only as payment references. It also presents gross and net derivative receivables and payables by contract type and hedge designation for both years, notes that structured notes are excluded, and describes netting under legally enforceable master netting agreements, including related cash collateral.

Explains fair-value recognition of freestanding derivatives, balance-sheet offsetting under enforceable netting agreements, and how hedge designation affects accounting and earnings. It covers fair value, cash flow, and net investment hedge requirements and treatment, effectiveness testing, discontinuation, OCI/AOCI and basis adjustments, plus derivative uses and disclosures. It reports 2025 and 2024 notionals by contract type, clarifies that notionals are activity measures rather than likely losses, and presents gross and net receivables and payables by type and designation, including collateral and netting; structured notes are excluded from these amounts.

nodes.title: Free-standing derivatives
key_items: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated balance sheets
nodes.summary: The notes disclose derivative receivables and payables on the consolidated balance sheets at December 31, 2025 and 2024, by contract type and hedge designation, showing gross trading balances, designated-hedge amounts, totals, and net balances. Structured notes elected under the fair value option are excluded. Under U.S. GAAP, balances and related cash collateral are netted when legally enforceable master netting agreements exist. Additional collateral disclosures explain that eligible liquid securities and cash held at third-party custodians are shown separately up to fair value exposure, while excess collateral and collateral lacking an appropriate legal opinion are excluded.

nodes.title: Derivatives netting and collateral
nodes.summary: The disclosure presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2025 and 2024 derivative receivables and payables by contract and settlement type, showing gross balances, amounts offset on the balance sheet, net balances, collateral, and resulting net amounts. Offsetting requires an appropriate legal opinion on the master netting agreement; otherwise balances remain separate. Additional collateral is excluded when held by third-party custodians, exceeding counterparty exposure, or tied to agreements lacking a legal opinion, subject to stated reporting limits. Tables cover interest-rate, credit, foreign-exchange, equity, and commodity contracts and distinguish OTC, OTC-cleared, and exchange-traded instruments. Notes explain daily settlement of futures, collateral eligibility and limits, and cash collateral netted against derivatives in both years.

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes derivative counterparty credit risk and mitigants (enforceable netting and collateral agreements), and liquidity risk from collateral posting and downgrade-triggered contract termination. At December 31, 2025 and 2024, net payables on OTC and OTC-cleared derivatives with downgrade features were $19.986 billion and $20.555 billion, with collateral posted of $15.371 billion and $15.204 billion, respectively. The text also reports additional collateral and termination-settlement impacts under single- and two-notch downgrades, noting that impacts generally arise only when ratings fall below contract thresholds; a single-agency downgrade may have no effect if another agency’s rating remains higher. Figures exclude posted collateral from termination amounts, while additional collateral includes initial margin.

nodes.title: Derivatives designated as hedges
Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: The notes explain that derivatives expose JPMorganChase to counterparty credit risk on receivables and liquidity risk on payables, which may require collateral as values shift or ratings fall. The Firm uses enforceable netting and collateral agreements to mitigate credit risk. Tables report 2025 and 2024 net OTC and OTC-cleared derivative payables with downgrade-triggered collateral or termination features and collateral posted, plus the liquidity impact of one- and two-notch downgrades: additional collateral required and fair value of contracts requiring settlement. A downgrade below the contract’s lowest current agency rating may trigger these obligations; a single-agency downgrade generally does not unless it breaches that threshold, with some initial-margin exceptions.

nodes.title: Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
nodes.summary:
Impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income
The following tables provide information related to gains and losses recorded on derivatives based on their hedge accounting designation or purpose.

nodes.title: Fair value hedge gains and losses
nodes.summary: The text reports JPMorgan Chase’s fair value hedge results for 2023–2025 by interest-rate, foreign-exchange and commodity contract, including derivative and hedged-item income effects, excluded-component amortization and fair-value changes, and OCI effects; gains and losses are presented in the same income-statement lines as hedged items. It explains hedge types, accounting treatment and excluded components. It also gives 2025 and 2024 carrying amounts and active, discontinued and total cumulative basis adjustments for AFS securities, long-term debt and VIE interests, expected to affect future yields, with notes on excluded commodities and currency-only hedges, portfolio-layer hedges, and how adjustment signs affect net interest income.

nodes.title: Cash flow hedge gains and losses
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023–2025 derivative gains and losses for cash flow hedges, including amounts reclassified from AOCI, recorded in OCI, related contract types, income-statement classifications, and expected future recognition; no forecasted transactions failed. It also presents net investment hedge results and related exclusions and reclassifications. It summarizes results and purposes of non-designated derivatives used for specified risk management, covering interest rate, credit, foreign exchange and equity risks, then describes market-making and other derivatives, their risk-management role and principal-transactions revenue classification.

Covers derivatives’ counterparty credit and liquidity risks, mitigation through netting and collateral agreements, and collateral or settlement obligations triggered by rating downgrades. It presents income-statement effects by hedge designation and purpose, including 2023–2025 fair value and cash flow hedge gains and losses, accounting treatment, excluded components, OCI and AOCI effects, future recognition, and cumulative basis adjustments. It also summarizes net investment hedges and non-designated risk-management, market-making, and other derivatives, including their purposes and income-statement classifications.

nodes.title: Risk management derivatives gains and losses
nodes.summary: The notes report pre-tax gains and losses on foreign-exchange derivatives in net investment hedge relationships for 2025–2023, including excluded forward-point amounts recorded in net interest income and gains or losses reclassified from AOCI upon sales or liquidations. They also present 2025–2023 income results for non-hedge-accounting derivatives used to manage specified interest-rate, credit, foreign-exchange, and equity risks, with related revenue classifications and risk-management purposes. Finally, they describe derivatives used in market-making and other activities, including counterparty credit-risk management; their results are primarily recorded in principal transactions revenue.

nodes.title: Market-making derivative gains and losses
key_items: Net investment hedge gains and losses
Gains and losses on derivatives used for specified risk management purposes
nodes.summary: The notes report 2025–2023 gains and losses on foreign-exchange derivatives used in net investment hedges, including accounting treatment and amounts reclassified from AOCI. They summarize 2025–2023 income effects of non-hedge-accounting derivatives used for specified interest-rate, credit, foreign-exchange and equity risk management, with related purposes and income classifications. They describe market-making and other derivatives and introduce credit derivatives: their risks and the Firm’s market-maker and end-user uses; single-name, index and tranche credit default swaps and settlement; credit-related notes and settlement; and how protection sold and purchased, recovery values and related positions are managed and summarized in tables.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
Credit default swaps
nodes.summary: Credit derivatives transfer third-party credit risk from protection purchasers to sellers, who receive premiums but face losses after events such as bankruptcy, nonpayment, or restructuring; purchasers also bear seller-credit risk. The Firm both trades protection as a client-serving market-maker and uses it to manage lending, counterparty, and market-making credit exposures. CDS may reference single entities, broad indices, or customized portfolios and tranches; single-name and index contracts can be OTC or cleared. Indices periodically update their constituents, removing entities after credit events. At settlement, purchasers claim the face-value/recovery-value difference from sellers, need not own the underlying debt, and have no recourse to the reference entity.

nodes.title: Credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Credit-related notes are funded derivatives in which investors provide par value and receive periodic credit-linked payments and principal at maturity, except after a specified credit event, when settlement reflects the reference obligation’s recovery value; neither party has recourse to the defaulting entity. The text introduces year-end 2025 and 2024 summaries of credit derivatives and notes sold and purchased, explains that protection sellers’ payouts typically reflect recoveries, and describes the Firm’s hedging through similar or related protection, including CIB notes and protection for retained loans. Notional amounts are not the Firm’s primary risk measure because they omit event probability, recovery value, and related instruments and hedges.

nodes.title: Total credit derivatives and credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Presents 2025 and 2024 credit derivative and credit-related note exposures (millions), including protection sold, purchased against identical underlyings, net protection, and other protection purchased. Notes define other derivatives, credit-related notes, matched-underlying protection, net amounts’ exclusion of settlement fair value effects, and other purchased protection. It also introduces tables summarizing protection-seller credit derivatives by reference-entity rating, remaining contractual maturity, and total fair value, noting purchaser profiles are comparable.

nodes.title: Protection sold – credit derivatives ratings (a) /maturity profile December 31, 2025 (in millions)
nodes.summary: The table reports protection sold through credit derivatives by reference-entity rating and maturity at December 31, 2025 and 2024, including investment-grade and noninvestment-grade notional amounts for under one year, one to five years, over five years, and in total. It also gives gross fair-value receivables, payables, and net fair value for both years. Ratings are primarily based on S&P and Moody’s external scales; fair values are before legally enforceable master-netting agreements, including cash-collateral netting.

Explains credit default swaps and credit-related notes, including how they transfer credit risk, their uses, reference structures, settlement, and seller and purchaser risks. Describes the Firm’s trading and hedging activities and why notionals alone do not measure risk. nodes.title: Note 12 - Loans
Loan accounting framework
key_items: Interest income; Allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: Note 12 explains loan accounting by management strategy: held-for-investment, held-for-sale, or fair value. It covers amortized-cost measurement and interest recognition; nonaccrual triggers, treatment of accrued interest, cash-basis recognition, and return to accrual; expected-credit-loss allowances and charge-offs, including delinquency timelines, exceptions, wholesale practices, and collateral valuation methods. Held-for-sale loans use lower of cost or fair value, while fair-value-option loans are marked to fair value; both accrue contractual interest, are subject to nonaccrual rules, and are excluded from allowance and charge-off policies.

nodes.title: Loan classification changes
nodes.summary: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value; credit losses reduce the loan-loss allowance, while noncredit losses enter noninterest revenue. Loans moved back to held-for-investment are recorded at amortized cost and assessed for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology. To mitigate losses, the Firm modifies loans for financially distressed borrowers through concessions such as rate reductions, extensions, payment delays, or principal forgiveness. Modified loans generally enter nonaccrual status, except certain current loans; accrual may resume after at least six months or six payments of performance and when repayment is reasonably assured. Allowances for modified loans use the established methodology and expected default rates.

nodes.title: Foreclosed property

It recognizes property when received in satisfaction of a loan, generally at a real-property foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu execution. Assets are reported in other assets and initially measured at fair value less estimated selling costs; each quarter they are reviewed and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value. Subsequent valuation changes affect noninterest revenue, while costs such as property taxes and maintenance are recorded as other expense.
