It describes retained interests, servicing and decision-making roles, consolidation criteria, restricted assets, credit support, commitments, and maximum loss exposure. It compares year-end balances across 2024 and 2025, including credit-card interests, securitization assets and exposures, re-securitization holdings, conduit paper and facilities, and municipal trust structures; it also explains customer versus non-customer sponsorship and related consolidation.

nodes.title: Consolidated VIE assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: The table reports assets and liabilities of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated VIEs by program type at December 31, 2025 and 2024, including trading assets, loans, other assets, beneficial interests and other liabilities. It notes mortgage securitizations include residential mortgages; certain loans are primarily CIB consumer loans; other assets include cash and balance-sheet items. VIE assets settle their liabilities; figures include third-party balances and exclude eliminated intercompany amounts. Beneficial-interest holders generally lack recourse to the Firm’s general credit; long-term beneficial interests were $6.0 billion in 2025 and $5.5 billion in 2024. Other liabilities are accounts payable and other balance-sheet liabilities.

nodes.title: VIEs sponsored by third parties
nodes.summary: The text describes the Firm’s involvement in third-party-sponsored VIEs, which are generally not consolidated when it lacks decision-making power or significant variable interests, and reports them like other third-party transactions. It covers unconsolidated tax-credit partnerships, their project types, control, tax-credit returns, maximum loss exposure and unfunded commitments, risk controls, and proportional amortization accounting, including eligibility, deferred taxes, contribution liabilities, reevaluation, and 2023–2025 financial data and exclusions. It also explains customer municipal bond TOB services, reimbursement agreements, nonprotection of residual holders, nonconsolidation, and maximum exposure and VIE asset fair values for 2024–2025.

nodes.title: Loan securitizations
nodes.summary: The Firm securitizes and sells residential and commercial mortgages, credit card receivables, and other consumer loans to meet investor demand and generate liquidity. For trusts it does not consolidate, it records a sale only when assets are legally isolated from creditors, transferees can pledge or exchange them, and the Firm lacks effective control. Sale gains or losses equal proceeds received—including cash, beneficial interests, or servicing assets—less the assets’ carrying value, and are reported as noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Securitization activity
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023–2025 securitization activity for unconsolidated, Firm-sponsored entities where sale accounting applied, including principal securitized, cash flows, loan-sale proceeds, servicing fees, and retained-interest valuation assumptions (weighted-average lives and discount rates). It describes nonrecourse mortgage and excess-MSR sales, mainly to U.S. GSEs, and Ginnie Mae transactions, noting guarantees, limited shared credit risk, nonconsolidation, and related indemnification disclosures. It summarizes loan-sale carrying values, cash and securities proceeds, and gains or losses. It also explains options to repurchase delinquent government-backed loans and reports repurchased or eligible loans, real estate owned, and foreclosed guaranteed mortgages for 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Loan delinquencies and liquidation losses
nodes.summary: The table reports components and delinquencies of loans in Firm-sponsored, nonconsolidated securitizations where the Firm had continuing involvement at year-end 2025 and 2024. It presents securitized residential mortgage loans (prime/Alt-A and option ARMs, and subprime), commercial and other loans, total securitized loans, 90-day-past-due balances, and net liquidation losses or recoveries. The text notes that servicing-only involvement generally exposes the Firm to losses only when repurchase is required for breaches of representations and warranties.

Explains the Firm’s accounting for and involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), including sponsored and third-party-sponsored structures, consolidation criteria, retained interests, servicing and decision-making roles, restricted assets, credit support, commitments, and maximum loss exposure. Reports 2024–2025 consolidated VIE assets and liabilities and exposures across securitizations, conduits, municipal vehicles, tax-credit partnerships, and customer transactions. Covers loan-sale accounting, securitization activity and proceeds, servicing and retained-interest valuation, government-backed loan repurchases and guarantees, and delinquency and liquidation-loss data for nonconsolidated securitizations.

nodes.title: Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets
Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets (intro)
nodes.summary: Goodwill arises from business combinations, may be adjusted for acquisition-date information during the following year, is allocated to reporting units, and is not amortized but tested annually in the fourth quarter or when impairment indicators arise. Tables show segment goodwill and changes for 2023–2025, including acquisitions, currency adjustments, and an immaterial 2025 impairment write-off. No impairment was identified at year-end in any of those years. Testing compares reporting-unit fair value with carrying value, using allocated capital as a carrying-value proxy and primarily discounted cash-flow valuations, supported by market comparables and comparison with firmwide market capitalization. Deteriorating performance, credit, capital, economic, regulatory, or equity-cost conditions could cause future impairment.

nodes.title: Mortgage servicing rights
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s mortgage servicing rights (MSRs): how they are recognized, measured at fair value using an option-adjusted spread model, and affected by servicing cash flows, assumptions and interest rates. It describes MSR interest-rate risk and hedging, provides 2023–2025 MSR activity, servicing income, serviced-loan and advance figures with related footnotes, and breaks down mortgage fees and servicing revenue, including risk-management impacts. It also presents 2024–2025 key valuation assumptions and fair-value sensitivities to adverse changes in prepayment speeds and discount spreads, noting that assumption effects may be interrelated and nonlinear.

nodes.title: Other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Other intangible assets are initially recorded at fair value, primarily in business combinations. Finite-lived assets, including core deposit and customer relationship intangibles, are amortized over expected-benefit useful lives; indefinite-lived assets, such as asset management contracts, are not amortized and are tested for impairment. At year-end 2025 versus 2024, gross carrying value was $3.5 billion versus $3.8 billion, accumulated amortization $962 million versus $879 million, finite-lived net value $1.3 billion versus $1.7 billion, and indefinite-lived net value $1.3 billion versus $1.2 billion. 2025 assets included First Republic-related customer intangibles and CIFM asset management contracts. Amortization expense was $292 million in 2025 and $339 million in 2024; estimated expense for 2026–2030 is $266 million, $264 million, $264 million, $252 million, and $100 million. Assets are assessed annually or when impairment indicators arise; impairment is charged to other expense.

Covers goodwill, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), and other intangible assets. Goodwill allocation, annual impairment testing, valuation methods, 2023–2025 balances and changes, and potential impairment drivers are described. MSR recognition, fair-value measurement, interest-rate risk and hedging, activity, servicing income and loan data, mortgage revenue, valuation assumptions, and sensitivities to prepayments and discount spreads are presented. Other intangible assets’ recognition, amortization and impairment policies, 2024–2025 balances and examples, historical amortization expense, and estimated 2026–2030 expense are also summarized.

nodes.title: Note 16 - Premises and equipment
nodes.summary: Premises and equipment comprises land at cost; buildings, leasehold improvements, internal-use software, and furniture and equipment at cost less depreciation or amortization; and operating lease right-of-use assets. At December 31, 2025 and 2024, total assets were $36.244 billion and $32.223 billion, respectively, including land, buildings and leasehold improvements, right-of-use assets, and other equipment/software. Additional right-of-use assets of $477 million and $564 million were reported in Other assets. Depreciation and amortization use straight-line methods; leasehold improvements are depreciated over the shorter of the remaining lease term or useful life. Software development costs are capitalized and amortized once ready for use. Useful lives are 10–50 years for buildings and improvements and 3–10 years for software and equipment. Impairment is assessed when events or circumstances suggest an asset may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: Note 17 - Deposits
nodes.summary: Note 17 reports deposits at December 31, 2025 and 2024: total deposits were $2,559,320 million and $2,406,032 million, respectively, with noninterest- and interest-bearing balances detailed for U.S. and non-U.S. offices. Fair-value amounts include structured notes classified as deposits under the fair value option. Deposits meeting or exceeding insured limits totaled $244,199 million in 2025 and $241,878 million in 2024; all non-U.S. time deposits are treated as exceeding the limit. The note also lists 2025 interest-bearing time-deposit maturities by year and office, totaling $311,400 million.

nodes.title: Note 18 - Leases
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s 2025 lease note describes its lessee accounting, primarily for operating leases: terms and options, recognition and measurement of liabilities and right-of-use assets, component elections, expense treatment, and absence of restrictive covenants. It reports lease balances, terms, discount rates, cash flows, new assets, rental expense, future payments, and $1.9 billion of signed, not-yet-commenced commitments. As lessor, the Firm describes auto and equipment lease accounting, depreciation, income, impairment and residual-value risk management, and reports asset carrying values, lease income, depreciation, and future receipts.

nodes.title: Note 19 - Accounts payable and other liabilities
nodes.summary: Accounts payable and other liabilities include brokerage payables to customers and for unsettled security purchases; accrued expenses such as compensation, credit card rewards, interest, merchant servicing and income taxes; and other liabilities, including operating leases, securities-return obligations measured at fair value, lending-commitment allowances and litigation reserves. Totals were $316.8 billion at December 31, 2025, versus $280.7 billion in 2024; brokerage payables were $186.7 billion and $153.2 billion, respectively, and other payables and liabilities were $130.1 billion and $127.5 billion. Credit card rewards liabilities were $16.0 billion and $14.4 billion. They reflect estimated redemption costs, accrue as rewards are earned, decline upon redemption, depend on redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions, and affect Card Income. Related details are referenced in Notes 7, 13, 18, 25 and 30.

nodes.title: Note 20 - Long-term debt
nodes.summary: Note 20 summarizes JPMorganChase’s long-term debt by issuer, type, currency-related interest characteristics, and remaining maturity for 2025 and 2024, including carrying values, rates, and beneficial interests. It explains fair-value accounting and DVA presentation; identifies secured, fair-value, zero-coupon, callable debt and annual maturities; and describes First Republic’s Purchase Money Note and beneficial-interest exclusions. It reports weighted-average rates before and after derivatives, subsidiary debt guarantees, and confirms unsecured debt has no specified rating- or financial-condition-triggered acceleration, borrowing-limit, or collateral requirements.

nodes.title: Note 21 - Preferred stock
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s preferred-stock note describes its authorization of 200 million $1-par shares and preferred holders’ priority over common stock in liquidation. It summarizes outstanding non-cumulative series, share counts, carrying values, issue and earliest redemption dates, contractual and floating rates, and declared dividends for 2023–2025, with terms explaining depositary shares, rate conversions, benchmarks, and discretionary, non-cumulative payment schedules. Each share has a $10,000 liquidation value and redemption price; aggregate liquidation value was $20.1 billion at year-end 2025. The note records 2024–2025 issuances and redemptions and explains redemption rights, including Federal Reserve non-objection requirements.

nodes.title: Note 22 - Common stock
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase was authorized to issue 9.0 billion $1-par common shares at year-end 2025 and 2024. The note reports 2023–2025 share balances, treasury-stock repurchases and reissuances, and year-end shares outstanding. A new $50 billion repurchase authorization began July 1, 2025, replacing the prior program’s authority of up to $30 billion through June 30. Annual repurchases and purchase prices are listed, excluding excise tax and commissions. Management controls timing and amount based on market, regulatory, capital and investment factors; purchases may vary, be suspended, or use open-market, private, or Rule 10b5-1 transactions. About 50 million shares were reserved for employee and director plans at year-end 2025.

nodes.title: Note 23 - Earnings per share
nodes.summary: Note 23 explains that basic EPS uses the two-class method, allocating earnings to common stock and participating securities; unvested RSUs with nonforfeitable dividend rights are treated as participating securities, while participating securities are excluded from diluted shares. Diluted EPS includes potentially issuable shares and uses the more dilutive result of the two-class and treasury stock methods; the two-class method was more dilutive in all periods shown. The table reports 2025, 2024 and 2023 net income, preferred dividends, earnings allocated to participating securities, applicable common earnings, weighted-average basic and diluted shares, dilutive awards, and basic and diluted EPS.

nodes.title: Note 24 - Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.summary: Note 24 defines AOCI as after-tax changes from investment securities, currency translation and related derivatives, excluded fair-value hedge components, cash-flow hedges, pension/OPEB plans, and own-credit-risk changes on fair-value-option liabilities. It presents component balances and movements for 2023–2025 and pre-tax, tax, and after-tax OCI changes for 2023–2025, including investment gains, translation and hedges, pension/OPEB, and DVA. A footnote details unrealized losses on securities transferred between AFS and HTM; other notes explain income-statement reclassifications, translation-hedge gains/losses, cross-currency basis-spread accounting, and where cash-flow hedge amounts are recorded.

nodes.title: Note 25 - Income taxes
Effective tax rate and expense
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes its consolidated U.S. tax filing, asset-and-liability accounting for current and deferred taxes, valuation allowances, and uncertainty in tax estimates across jurisdictions. It notes adoption of updated income-tax disclosure and tax-credit investment standards. Disclosures compare 2025–2023 statutory and effective tax rates and reconciling items; current and deferred tax expense, including audit-resolution benefits; tax effects recorded directly in equity; U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income; and income taxes paid by jurisdiction, with amounts and threshold-based “not meaningful” categories.

nodes.title: Results from Non-U.S. earnings
nodes.summary: The text reports income tax expense by current and deferred U.S. federal, state/local, and non-U.S. components for 2025–2023, totaling $15.547 billion, $16.610 billion, and $12.060 billion; these totals include tax-audit resolution benefits of $629 million, $314 million, and $68 million. It explains excluded stockholders’ equity tax effects, including 2024 and 2023 accounting-guidance adoptions. It gives U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income and defines non-U.S. income and the treatment of global intangible low-tax income. It also reports net cash income taxes paid by jurisdiction, totaling $5.309 billion, $11.715 billion, and $9.908 billion, and explains the 5% reporting threshold and “NM” designation.

nodes.title: Deferred taxes
key_items: Tax effect of items recorded in stockholders’ equity
Results from U.S. and non-U.S. earnings
nodes.summary: The excerpt details JPMorgan Chase’s 2023–2025 income tax expense by current and deferred U.S. federal, state/local, and non-U.S. components, including tax-audit resolution benefits and equity-recorded tax effects from accounting-guidance adoptions. It reports U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income and defines non-U.S. income, then summarizes cash income taxes paid by jurisdiction. It explains deferred-tax recognition and valuation allowances and presents deferred tax assets and liabilities, net balances, tax-attribute carryforwards, their amounts and expiration periods, and the main drivers of the 2025 valuation allowance.

nodes.title: Unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase reported unrecognized tax benefits of $5.6 billion, $6.2 billion and $5.4 billion at year-end 2025, 2024 and 2023; $4.6 billion, $4.4 billion and $3.9 billion, respectively, would reduce the effective tax rate if recognized. Other items would have no effective-rate impact because of temporary differences or tax offsets. The Firm reassesses benefits based on expected tax positions and ongoing audits, notably by the IRS. A reconciliation shows annual increases and decreases from current- and prior-period positions and cash settlements. After-tax interest and penalties recognized in tax expense were $241 million, $288 million and $229 million for 2025–2023; accrued tax-related interest and penalties were $1.9 billion and $1.7 billion at year-end 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: Tax examination status
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase reports ongoing tax examinations by U.S., New York City and State, and U.K. authorities, covering specified tax years from 2011–2023, with matters at field examination or appellate stages. The notes describe regulatory restrictions on cash and assets, including $29.0 billion of restricted cash in 2025 ($27.5 billion in 2024), plus customer-related pledged cash and securities. They explain legal limits on bank-affiliate transactions, intercompany funding and dividends, regulatory authority to restrict dividends, IHC capital and liquidity constraints, and the bank’s approximately $30.1 billion dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2026.

The note covers JPMorganChase’s income-tax accounting, estimates, disclosures and effective tax-rate reconciliations for 2023–2025, including current and deferred expense, audit-resolution benefits, equity-recorded tax effects, pretax income, and taxes paid by jurisdiction. It details deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances and tax-attribute carryforwards; unrecognized tax benefits, interest, penalties and audit-related changes; and tax examinations by U.S., New York and U.K. authorities. It also describes restricted cash and securities, limits on affiliate transactions and funding, dividend restrictions, IHC constraints and bank dividend capacity.

nodes.title: Note 26 - Restrictions on cash and intercompany funds transfers
key_items: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
nodes.summary: Note 26 describes regulatory restrictions on cash and assets, including bank reserve requirements and broker-dealer safeguards. Restricted cash totaled $29.0 billion in 2025 versus $27.5 billion in 2024, with details on customer-segregated funds and central-bank reserves; other restricted assets included pledged cash and securities and securities related to customer activity. It also explains legal limits on bank lending and other transactions with affiliates, the roles and funding relationships of the Parent Company and intermediate holding company, regulator authority to restrict dividends, IHC thresholds, and the bank’s approximately $30.1 billion dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2026.

nodes.title: Note 27 - Regulatory capital
nodes.summary: The note explains Federal Reserve and OCC Basel III capital oversight, Standardized and Advanced RWA methods, and minimum risk-based and leverage ratios for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. It lists 2025 requirements and well-capitalized thresholds, related buffers, surcharges, and 2024 requirement changes. It describes the CECL transition’s full phaseout by January 2025 and reports 2025 and 2024 capital amounts, RWA, risk-based ratios, leverage ratios, and SLRs, including Apple Card and First Republic effects. Both entities met all applicable requirements and were well-capitalized.

nodes.title: Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments (intro)
nodes.summary: Note 28 explains that JPMorganChase provides lending commitments and guarantees to meet customer financing needs. Contractual amounts reflect maximum potential credit risk but are not considered representative of expected exposure or funding needs, since instruments are often unused, renewed, canceled, or expire without default. The Firm maintains an allowance for expected losses on wholesale and certain consumer commitments (see Note 13). A table presents contractual amounts and carrying values for 2025 and 2024; certain card, home-equity, and business-banking figures represent total available credit. The Firm does not expect all lines to be used simultaneously and may reduce or cancel commitments under contract or law, including after credit deterioration or falling property values.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports 2025 and 2024 off-balance-sheet lending-related commitments, guarantees and other obligations by maturity, contractual amount and carrying value, with notes on consumer and wholesale categories, risk participations, collateral, clearing-house guarantees, Apple Card exposure and carrying-value accounting. It explains the nature of unfunded credit commitments and U.S. GAAP guarantee recognition, including initial fair-value liabilities and subsequent treatment of contingent obligations and indemnifications. It also defines standby letters of credit and presents their contractual amounts, carrying values, collateral, allowances and guarantee liabilities by internal credit rating.

nodes.title: Credit Commitments and Guarantees
key_items: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
nodes.summary: Describes unfunded credit commitments for working capital, corporate purposes, commercial paper and bond support, clearing liquidity, and multipurpose facilities. Explains U.S. GAAP guarantee definitions and accounting: initial fair-value recognition, premium treatment and amortization, and recognition of contingent obligations and indemnifications. Notes that guarantee amounts and carrying values are reported in a separate table, and describes standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees as conditional commitments supporting clients’ obligations in financing and trade transactions.

nodes.title: Standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and other letters of credit
key_items: Securities lending indemnifications; Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
nodes.summary: The text reports 2025 and 2024 amounts for standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and letters of credit, including investment-grade and noninvestment-grade totals, carrying values, allowances, guarantee liabilities, and collateralized commitments; ratings use the Firm’s internal scale. It explains securities-lending indemnifications, daily collateralization above 100%, and remedies for borrower defaults, plus protections for invested cash collateral. It describes written-put and stable-value derivative guarantees, their terms, exposure and fair-value measurement, and hedging. A table gives 2025/2024 notionals, limited stable-value exposures, and fair values; credit derivatives are also noted.

nodes.title: Unsettled securities financing agreements
nodes.summary: The Firm enters into future-settling resale and securities-borrowed agreements, under which it advances cash and receives securities collateral, and repurchase and securities-loaned agreements, under which it receives cash and provides collateral. These agreements generally are not derivatives and are not recorded on the Consolidated balance sheets until settlement; most have regular-way settlement terms. See Note 11 for further discussion.

nodes.title: Loan sales- and securitization-related indemnifications
key_items: Private label securitizations; Loans sold with recourse
nodes.summary: The Firm’s mortgage loan sales to U.S. GSEs include representations and warranties that may require repurchase or indemnification if breached. Private-label securitization repurchase demands are evaluated separately in litigation reserves (see Note 30). Mortgage servicing may be recourse or nonrecourse: nonrecourse risk mainly involves temporary servicing advances, while recourse entails sharing credit losses with loan owners when foreclosure proceeds are insufficient. Most Firm securitizations are nonrecourse, transferring future credit-loss risk to securities purchasers. The unpaid balance of recourse loans and related recorded liability are disclosed on page 296.

nodes.title: Other off-balance sheet arrangements
key_items: Exchange & Clearing House Memberships; Sponsored member repo program
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s off-balance-sheet arrangements and related risks: tax-related and business indemnifications, merchant charge-backs and mitigants, client credit exposure from clearing services, and potential obligations from exchange and clearing-house memberships. It also covers guarantees of sponsored-member repo clients, secured by collateral, and Parent Company guarantees of subsidiary obligations and debt, including JPMFC securities. Maximum exposures can be difficult to estimate; management generally considers losses remote, and applicable disclosures and notes are referenced.

Note 28 covers the Firm’s lending commitments, guarantees and other off-balance-sheet arrangements, including contractual amounts, carrying values, maturities, collateral, allowances and credit ratings for 2025 and 2024. It explains expected exposure and usage, commitment cancellation, guarantee accounting, standby letters and other financial guarantees, securities-lending indemnities, written-put and stable-value guarantees, and credit derivatives. It also describes unsettled securities-financing agreements, mortgage-sale and securitization indemnifications, servicing recourse, merchant charge-backs, clearing and exchange obligations, sponsored-member repo guarantees, and Parent Company guarantees, with related risk mitigants and disclosures.

nodes.title: Note 29 - Pledged assets and collateral
nodes.summary: Note 29 describes the Firm’s pledged assets and accepted collateral. Pledged assets support borrowing capacity at Federal Reserve banks, other central banks and FHLBs, and collateralize securities financing, short sales, derivatives and deposits; some may be sold, repledged or otherwise used by secured parties. Total pledged assets were $1,333.6 billion in 2025 versus $1,174.4 billion in 2024, comprising assets usable by secured parties ($185.6 billion/$152.5 billion), assets not so usable ($410.9 billion/$297.9 billion), and assets pledged at Federal Reserve banks and FHLBs ($737.1 billion/$724.0 billion). By type, 2025/2024 pledged assets were investment securities ($82.7/$89.6 billion), loans ($763.8/$740.9 billion), and trading assets and other ($487.1/$343.9 billion). Totals exclude assets of consolidated VIEs, with related details referenced in Notes 14, 11 and 20. The Firm accepts collateral, generally under resale and securities financing agreements, prime brokerage customer receivables and derivatives, and uses it for financing, short sales, derivatives and deposits. Fair value of collateral permitted to be used was $1,771.0 billion in 2025 and $1,544.0 billion in 2024; amounts actually sold, repledged, delivered or otherwise used were $1,426.4 billion and $1,210.7 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Note 30 - Litigation
Fair Access to Banking
nodes.summary: As of December 31, 2025, the Firm faced numerous private, public, governmental and regulatory proceedings across businesses and geographies, involving varied claims and stages. Estimated reasonably possible losses above reserves were $0–$1.2 billion where estimable; uncertainty, unresolved issues and judgment mean estimates may change and actual losses may differ. Material matters include India’s ED investigation and appealed $31.5 million fine related to Amrapali housing investments, and responses to government inquiries following the 2025 fair-banking executive order, including reviews, investigations and a January 2026 Florida lawsuit by President Trump and affiliated entities.

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s FX matters, including its 2015 antitrust guilty plea, DOL exemption, pending South African inquiry, overseas civil actions, and related settlements and class-certification rulings. It summarizes interchange-fee litigation, settlements, remaining merchant claims, and a 2026 trial; LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations and appeals, including dismissal of U.S. LIBOR claims subject to appeal; and Russian sanctions-related litigation, judgments, asset freezes, appeals, and risk of seizure of Russian and client assets.

nodes.title: Antitrust and Benchmark-Rate Litigation
key_items: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
nodes.summary: The text notes pending foreign FX-related civil actions, a U.K. ruling denying opt-out class certification, and an Israeli settlement awaiting court approval. Interchange litigation includes a settled damages class, a proposed injunctive settlement revised and awaiting approval, and remaining merchant opt-out cases, with a trial scheduled for April 2026. Benchmark-rate matters include global LIBOR/EURIBOR inquiries, an EU fine reimposed after annulment and under appeal, and U.S. dollar LIBOR claims dismissed with prejudice in September 2025; plaintiffs appealed.

nodes.title: Russian Litigation
nodes.summary: The Firm must block assets under international sanctions and is contractually excused from certain Russia-related payments. Russian courts have disregarded forum-selection agreements and foreign sanctions, issuing judgments against the Firm, including one for $439 million, with enforcement stayed pending appeal, and another executed against onshore assets. Judgments exceed the Firm’s Russian assets; courts have also permitted clients’ dividends to be withheld and ordered interim freezes on assets. The Firm is appealing and challenging claims and freezes in contractually selected jurisdictions, but further enforcement could seize all Russian Firm assets and some client assets or prevent the Firm from meeting obligations.

nodes.title: Shareholder Litigation
nodes.summary: A shareholder derivative suit in the Eastern District of New York alleges misconduct tied to historical precious-metals and U.S. Treasury trading practices addressed in the Firm’s September 2020 DOJ, CFTC and SEC resolutions; defendants have moved to dismiss. JPMorganChase faces many other proceedings, asserts it has meritorious defenses, and intends to defend them. It maintains and quarterly reassesses reserves under U.S. GAAP, reporting legal expenses of $361 million, $740 million and $1.4 billion in 2025, 2024 and 2023. Outcomes, timing and losses remain uncertain; pending matters are not expected to materially affect consolidated financial condition, but could exceed reserves, harm reputation, or materially affect results in a period.

The section reviews JPMorgan Chase’s litigation and investigations as of December 31, 2025, including estimated reasonably possible losses above reserves of up to $1.2 billion and uncertainty in outcomes. Matters include India’s Amrapali investigation and fine; fair-banking inquiries and a January 2026 Florida lawsuit; foreign-exchange, interchange-fee and LIBOR/EURIBOR proceedings, settlements, appeals and a 2026 trial; Russian sanctions litigation, judgments, asset freezes and enforcement risks; and a shareholder derivative suit tied to past trading practices. It also describes defenses, reserves, legal expenses, and potential financial, reputational and period-specific impacts.

nodes.title: Note 31 - International operations
nodes.summary: Note 31 defines international operations as transactions involving clients outside the U.S., classified mainly by client domicile, relationship-management or booking location, or trading desk; U.S. operations also serve international businesses. Because operations are integrated, revenue and expense allocations rely on estimates consistent with segment reporting. Long-lived assets are not significant relative to total assets and are mostly in the U.S. The table reports 2023–2025 revenue, expense, pretax income, net income, and total assets by international region and North America. North America substantially reflects the U.S.; revenue includes net interest and noninterest revenue, while expense includes noninterest expense and credit-loss provisions. U.K. assets were approximately $449 billion, $369 billion, and $352 billion in 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively.

nodes.title: Note 32 - Business segments & Corporate
JPMorgan Chase Business Segments and Corporate
nodes.summary: The Firm is managed by lines of business, with three reportable segments and remaining activities in Corporate; segments reflect products, services, clients, and how results are evaluated, and are reported on a managed basis. Consumer & Community Banking serves consumers and small businesses through branches, ATMs, digital and phone channels, covering banking and wealth, mortgages, cards, and auto lending. Commercial & Investment Bank serves global corporate and institutional clients through Banking & Payments—investment banking, lending, payments, liquidity, trade and working capital—and Markets & Securities Services, including market-making, financing, risk management, prime brokerage, clearing, research, custody and related services. Asset & Wealth Management, with $7.1 trillion in client assets, provides investment management across asset classes and private-bank services such as retirement, brokerage, custody, estate planning, lending, deposits and wealth management. Corporate comprises Treasury and CIO, which manage liquidity, funding, capital and structural interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks, plus centrally managed staff, expenses, initiatives and functions including real estate, technology, legal, finance, HR, audit, risk, compliance and corporate responsibility.

nodes.title: Asset & Wealth Management
nodes.summary: The Firm reports results on a managed basis across three segments—Consumer & Community Banking (consumer and small-business banking, wealth, mortgages, cards and auto), Commercial & Investment Bank (investment banking, lending, payments, markets, financing, custody and securities services for corporate and institutional clients), and Asset & Wealth Management (asset management and private banking, with $7.1 trillion in client assets)—plus Corporate. Corporate includes Treasury and the Chief Investment Office, which manage liquidity, funding, capital and structural interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks, and centrally managed functions, expenses, initiatives and other activities. Segments reflect products, services and clients and are evaluated by the Operating Committee, the Firm’s collective chief decision maker.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF LISTED PREFERRED STOCK
nodes.summary: The text directs readers to the certificate of incorporation and series-specific certificates of designations for complete terms. The board may issue up to 200 million $1-par preferred shares in series and set their rights and restrictions; authorized shares may be amended as permitted. Of 11 outstanding series, six are SEC-registered Listed Preferred Stock series, each represented by depositary shares equal to 1/400 of a preferred share; these shares are fully paid and nonassessable. They rank equally with parity preferred stock, ahead of common and junior preferred stock, but behind indebtedness. Dividends are board-declared, noncumulative cash payments to record holders. Undeclared dividends are forfeited; full dividends on parity or junior stock generally require payment or provision for Listed Preferred Stock first, and partial parity dividends are allocated pro rata according to amounts due.

nodes.title: Preferred Stock Authorization, Outstanding Shares, and Ranking
nodes.summary: The certificate of incorporation authorizes the board to issue up to 200 million shares of preferred stock, set each series’ terms, and amend the authorized amount as permitted. At the Form 10-K filing date, 11 series were outstanding; six listed series are registered under Exchange Act Section 12, represented by depositary shares equal to 1/400 interests, and are fully paid and nonassessable. Their terms are summarized elsewhere. The listed shares rank pari passu with parity-ranking preferred stock, ahead of common and junior preferred stock, but behind existing and future indebtedness.

nodes.title: Dividend Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock dividends are board-declared, paid to record holders, and noncumulative, so undeclared dividends are forfeited. Full dividends must generally be paid or provided for before dividends on equal- or junior-ranking stock; partial parity dividends are allocated pro rata. Until preferred dividends are covered, junior-stock distributions and certain redemptions or purchases are restricted, subject to listed exceptions and ordinary-course market transactions. The text defines junior, parity, and senior ranking, permits eligible dividends on other stock without preferred participation, and specifies dividend calculation, day-count, and rounding rules.

nodes.title: Rights Upon Liquidation
nodes.summary: Upon liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, each Listed Preferred Stock series receives $10,000 per share plus declared, unpaid dividends before junior shareholders; undeclared dividends do not accumulate, and holders have no claim to remaining assets. If a series cannot be paid in full, it shares assets ratably with equally ranked stock. Asset sales and mergers or consolidations are not liquidation events. As a holding company, claims on subsidiary assets may be subject to subsidiary creditors’ priority. Listed Preferred holders rank behind the company’s debt and other non-equity claims, and may also rank behind U.S. government interests in insolvency or similar proceedings.

nodes.title: Redemption
nodes.summary: The text covers preferred-stock redemption terms, including scheduled and capital-treatment-event redemptions, regulatory approval, notice requirements, partial-redemption selection, dividend and rights termination, limits on redemption or repurchases when dividends are unpaid, and the absence of holder-initiated redemption. It states there are no preemptive or conversion rights and identifies Computershare as depositary, transfer agent, and registrar. Voting provisions include limited voting rights, director-election rights after six missed quarterly dividends and their termination, and approval thresholds for senior securities or adverse amendments, with specified actions deemed non-adverse.

nodes.title: Preferred Stock Rights and Administration
nodes.summary: On redemption, dividends on called shares accumulate through the redemption date, after which holders retain no rights except to receive the redemption price. If full dividends, including accumulated unpaid dividends, are unpaid, the series cannot be partially redeemed or acquired except through an offer on equal terms to all its holders. Listed Preferred Stock has no preemptive or conversion rights. Computershare Inc. serves as depositary, transfer agent, and registrar for each series and related depositary shares.

nodes.title: Voting Rights
nodes.summary: Listed Preferred Stock generally has no voting rights except as required by law or specified, with one vote per share (1/400 per depositary share) when voting applies. Six unpaid quarterly dividends trigger election of two preferred directors alongside voting parity stock; those rights end after four consecutive quarters of full dividends, subject to possible revival, and rules govern removal and vacancies. A two-thirds class vote is generally required to issue senior securities or adversely amend series rights, with specified exceptions and series-only approval when only one series is affected. Redemption with funds irrevocably placed in trust suspends these votes; additional shares may be issued without holder consent. Delaware-law class voting and charter provisions address amendments and share authorization. Federal Reserve rules may impose bank-holding-company regulation, approval, or notice requirements on significant holders when arrears grant director-election rights.

nodes.summary: Defines Closing Intrinsic Note Value as principal multiplied by the Index Ratio, plus a stub coupon, less any Investor Fee Shortfall, and including an unpaid prior coupon when its ex-date has not occurred. For measurement periods, it uses average VWAP Levels and the period’s final day for coupon-related calculations. This value is not a market trading price or offer; trading prices may differ due to supply and demand, liquidity, costs, credit, and spreads. Fee shortfalls reduce maturity, repurchase, or redemption payments. Defines the Index Ratio, initial VWAP level (260.0267), final VWAP level and five-business-day Measurement Period, including postponement for disruptions; explains VWAP Level, VWAP, Index Units, and Index Divisor, noting VWAP may differ from the official Index close and calculations may be modified. nodes.summary: Defines coupon-related terms for the Alerian ETNs: the 0.85% annual investor fee accrues daily, includes prior shortfalls, and is calculated using principal, the Index Ratio, and a 30/360 day-count fraction. The Reference Distribution Amount totals qualifying gross cash distributions during each accrual period, with unpaid distributions scheduled before the Coupon Ex-Date treated as zero. A hypothetical Reference Holder’s shares are based on Index Units and the Index Divisor, with reduced holdings applied on specified Measurement Period days for certain stub coupons. These amounts and holdings adjust for ETN splits or reverse splits. The text also specifies accrual periods, quarterly valuation dates, ex-date conventions (including a change expected from May 28, 2024), record dates, and payment dates, which may be postponed for market disruption.

nodes.title: Terms Relating to Issuer Redemption
nodes.summary: From July 26, 2024, the issuer may redeem all or part of the Alerian ETNs on any Business Day, giving DTC irrevocable notice at least five Business Days before the specified Redemption Valuation Date. For partial redemptions, the notice states the principal amount, and the Trustee selects notes fairly, such as pro rata or by lot. Holders receive cash on the Redemption Settlement Date equal to the Closing Intrinsic Note Value measured for that valuation date, or $0 if the value is nonpositive. Settlement usually follows the Measurement Period by the standard cycle (currently two Business Days, expected to become one on May 28, 2024), and cannot be more than five Business Days later.

nodes.title: Terms Relating to Weekly Repurchase Right
key_items: Early Repurchase; Payment upon Early Repurchase; Repurchase Fee Amount; Repurchase Date
nodes.summary: Holders may request weekly early repurchase of at least 50,000 Alerian ETNs, subject to adjustment for splits and required procedures, unless a notice to redeem all outstanding notes has been submitted. The issuer may reduce the minimum consistently for all holders but need not. Payment per ETN is closing intrinsic note value over the measurement period, less a fee of 0.125% of that value excluding unpaid coupons; amounts at or below zero result in no payment. Valuation is generally each Friday. Repurchase settlement follows the measurement period by the standard cycle (currently two business days, expected to become one on May 28, 2024), but no more than five business days. Requests require an issuer-form notice emailed by 4 p.m. New York time on the preceding business day, a delivery-versus-payment trade booked for the measurement period’s final day, and DTC settlement by 10 a.m. on the repurchase date. Brokerage deadlines may differ. Notices are irrevocable, effective only if timely received and acknowledged by the issuer or affiliate that same business day; the calculation agent decides validity and receipt-timing questions.

key_items: Split or Reverse Split of the Alerian ETNs
nodes.summary: Defines M1, M2, D1, and D2 for coupon accrual periods. The Issuer may split or reverse-split Alerian ETNs, setting the ratio and announcing the effective date at least three Business Days ahead; the record date is the preceding Business Day. It may adjust related ETN amounts, share counts, and repurchase minimums, including retroactive coupon adjustments. Reverse-split fractional holdings may be compensated at the calculation agent’s discretion; the Issuer currently intends cash compensation under specified timing and valuation rules. Coupon and maturity payments shift to the next Business Day when needed, or to the third Business Day after a postponed Averaging Date when it falls too close to payment; no interest accrues for delays.

nodes.title: Postponement of an Averaging Date
nodes.summary: The final VWAP level is the arithmetic average of five daily levels, with disrupted-component calculations postponed to prevent reusing a component’s VWAP for multiple averaging dates; no postponement extends beyond the third Index Business Day after the originally scheduled date. On an Unavailable Day, the level is an Adjusted VWAP Level: unaffected components use scheduled-date inputs, while affected components use the first subsequent available day’s inputs, or good-faith agent estimates if unavailable through the final disrupted date. Unavailable Days include disrupted days and prior valuation dates. A Disrupted Day involves an exchange closure or market disruption that the Note Calculation Agent determines materially affects the level.

nodes.title: Market Disruption Events
nodes.summary: A Market Disruption Event for an Index Component includes suspension, absence or limitation of component trading on its Primary Exchange; disruption of related futures or options trading on a Related Exchange; events impairing market participants’ ability to transact or obtain values; or an unannounced early exchange closure that fails the specified one-hour notice test. The Note Calculation Agent determines these matters in its sole discretion, and the event must materially interfere with the Issuer’s or an affiliate’s ability to adjust or unwind all or a material part of an Alerian ETN hedge. Announced changes to regular trading hours are excluded; trading restrictions under rules comparable to NYSE Rule 80B during significant market fluctuations count. Scheduled Closing Time is the exchange’s regular-session weekday close, excluding after-hours trading.

nodes.title: Discontinuation of the Index; Alteration of Method of Calculation
nodes.summary: If the Index is discontinued or its data become unavailable, the Note Calculation Agent may select a comparable successor index, apply a fixed adjustment to preserve continuity of VWAP levels, and notify the Trustee, Issuer and DTC. On default-related acceleration, the cash payment is calculated using the acceleration date and a five-Index-Business-Day measurement period, with no further accrual; payment details must be reported promptly, within two Business Days. The ETNs are listed on NYSE Arca as AMJB, but continued listing and liquidity are not assured. They are issued in book-entry form through DTC as global master notes, with investors’ beneficial interests recorded through intermediaries; “holders” refers to owners registered directly in the Issuer’s or paying agent’s records.

nodes.title: Denominations
nodes.summary: Alerian ETNs are issued in Principal Amount denominations. BNY Mellon or an affiliate handles registration and transfers, and BNY Mellon serves as paying agent; transfers are free except for applicable taxes or government charges. The issuer may issue fungible additional ETNs without notice or consent, but need not do so; issuance changes or suspensions can affect liquidity, trading prices, premiums, and outstanding amounts. The ETNs impose no limits on other issuer debt or securities, and the issuer need not consider holders’ interests. The text introduces the 2032 Callable Notes and summarizes their governing indenture: $5 million was outstanding at year-end 2024; they are unsecured, unsubordinated issuer obligations, fully guaranteed by JPMorgan Chase, and uninsured. Issued in $1,000 units in 2021, they mature in 2032, pay 2.60% interest semiannually, and may be redeemed in full in 2031 with notice. JPMS calculates payments; following default acceleration, holders receive principal plus accrued interest, with specified calculation and notice procedures.

nodes.title: Modification of the 2016 Indenture

nodes.title: Key Terms of the VYLD ETNs General
nodes.summary: VYLD ETNs have a $25 principal amount, adjustable for splits or reverse splits. They track the daily returns of an inverse, rolling short position in first- and second-month VIX futures, less a daily fee; the total-return index also accrues interest at SOFR. At maturity, holders receive the closing intrinsic note value unless the notes were previously redeemed or repurchased. After March 21, 2025, the issuer may redeem some or all notes on any business day for that value. Weekly, holders may request repurchase of at least 50,000 notes, subject to procedures and possible issuer waiver or reduction of the minimum; a 0.125% fee may apply. Repurchase proceeds equal the closing intrinsic note value less any fee, or zero if the result is nonpositive.

nodes.title: Terms Relating to Closing Intrinsic Note Value
key_items: Closing Intrinsic Note Value; Daily Index Factor; Daily Fee Deduction
nodes.summary: The Closing Intrinsic Note Value starts at the Principal Amount on March 19, 2025, then updates from the prior non-disrupted Index Business Day’s value multiplied by the Daily Index Factor, less the Daily Fee Deduction. If it reaches zero or less, it remains zero thereafter. It is not a secondary-market price or trading recommendation; actual trading prices may differ significantly for market, liquidity, volatility, cost, credit, and spread reasons. The value may be adjusted for ETN splits or reverse splits. The Daily Index Factor is the current Index closing level divided by that on the prior Calculation Day. The Daily Fee Deduction applies the 0.85% annual investor fee to the prior value using elapsed calendar days divided by 360.

nodes.title: Terms Relating to Issuer Redemption
key_items: Issuer Early Redemption; Payment upon Early Redemption
nodes.summary: After March 21, 2025, the issuer may redeem all or some VYLD ETNs on any Business Day, giving DTC at least five Business Days’ irrevocable notice before the specified Redemption Valuation Date. For partial redemptions, the trustee selects ETNs pro rata, by lot, or through another fair method. Holders receive cash per redeemed ETN equal to its Closing Intrinsic Note Value on the Redemption Valuation Date, which may be postponed for a Market Disruption Event. The Redemption Date normally follows the valuation date by one Business Day, or the standard settlement cycle, and may be no more than five Business Days later.

nodes.title: Terms Relating to Weekly Holder Repurchase
key_items: Holder Early Repurchase; Payment upon Early Repurchase; Repurchase Fee Amount; Repurchase Valuation Date; Repurchase Date; Repurchase Procedures
nodes.summary: The text explains weekly early repurchases of VYLD ETNs: holders may request repurchase of at least 50,000 notes (adjustable after splits and potentially reduced by the Issuer), unless a notice to redeem all outstanding notes has been submitted. Payment per note is the closing intrinsic value on the weekly valuation date, less a 0.125% fee unless waived, with a minimum payment of zero. Valuation is generally Friday; payment follows the standard settlement cycle, currently one business day, and no later than five business days. Requests require an Issuer-form notice emailed by 4 p.m. New York time on the preceding business day, a DTC delivery-versus-payment trade, and settlement delivery by 10 a.m. on the repurchase date. Broker deadlines may differ. Notices are irrevocable, must arrive by the deadline and receive same-day Issuer or affiliate acknowledgment; the Calculation Agent decides validity and receipt-timing disputes. Valuation may be postponed for market disruption.

A Disrupted Day involves a trading-session failure or continuing Market Disruption Event that the Note Calculation Agent deems materially affects the Index. S&P Dow Jones is Index Sponsor and Index Calculation Agent; JPMS is Note Calculation Agent; MerQube is Published ETN Value Calculation Agent; Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas is Trustee.

nodes.title: Note Calculation Agent, Index Calculation Agent and Published ETN Value Calculation Agent
nodes.summary: The issuer and JPMorganChase may replace any of the three calculation agents without holder consent or notice. The Note Calculation Agent handles VYLD ETN calculations and determinations not assigned to the others, including payments, pricing assumptions, and amendments or confirmations of intrinsic values; the Index Calculation Agent sets the closing index level each Index Business Day, subject to valuation-date postponement; and the Published ETN Value Calculation Agent calculates intrinsic values for publication. Their determinations are discretionary and, absent manifest error, conclusive and binding. The Note Calculation Agent must notify the Trustee of payments by 11:00 a.m. New York time on the payment date. Values are rounded to five decimal places; per-note payment amounts to four decimal places; and aggregate holder payments to cents, with specified ties rounded upward.

nodes.title: Split or Reverse Split of the VYLD ETNs
nodes.summary: The Issuer may split or reverse split VYLD ETNs, setting the ratio and giving holders notice at least three Business Days before effectiveness; it may adjust note values, fees, and repurchase minimums accordingly. Reverse-split fractional notes may be compensated at the Note Calculation Agent’s discretion; the Issuer currently intends cash compensation within specified time limits. Maturity may be postponed for non-Business Days or delayed valuation, without interest for delay. Disrupted valuation dates move to the next non-disrupted Index Business Day, subject to a three-day limit and a fallback calculation. Market disruption includes specified VIX futures trading, reporting, or market-access problems that materially impair hedging, but not announced trading-hour changes. If the Index ends, an acceptable successor may replace it with comparability adjustments and notice; absent one, the Agent determines the Index level under the existing calculation method.

nodes.title: Maturity, Valuation, and Market Disruption Rules
nodes.summary: The page explains maturity-date adjustments for non-Business Days and postponed Final Valuation Dates, including payment timing and no interest on delayed payments. It defines Market Disruption Events, including trading suspensions or limitations, reporting-system failures, and other market impairments that materially hinder hedging, as determined by the agent. nodes.title: Discontinuation of the Index; Alteration of Method of Calculation

Upon default acceleration, payment per ETN equals its Closing Intrinsic Note Value, adjusted for a disrupted day; this is final, with notice to the Trustee and DTC within two business days. VYLD is listed on NYSE Arca, but continued listing or liquidity is not assured. nodes.title: Denominations

The Bank of New York Mellon or an affiliate serves as registrar and transfer agent, and the Bank also serves as paying agent, with the option to appoint additional agents. Maturity payments and transfer registration are handled at its principal corporate trust office in New York City. Transfers are registered without charge, except for applicable taxes or government charges, for which indemnity may be required.

nodes.title: Governing Law
nodes.summary: VYLD ETNs are governed by New York law. The Issuer may, at its sole discretion and without notice or holder consent, issue, restrict, suspend, stop, or resume additional ETNs, but has no obligation to do so or consider holders’ interests. Changes in issuance can adversely affect liquidity and trading prices; resumed sales may erase premiums, exposing buyers who paid above intrinsic value to significant losses at sale, maturity, repurchase, or redemption. Holders should consult advisers, particularly when ETNs trade at a premium. Suspensions may also reduce outstanding notes if holders seek repurchase, causing note counts and liquidity to vary. Additional notes become interchangeable with the original sub-series, share its CUSIP, and increase its principal amount. The ETNs do not restrict the Issuer’s other borrowing or securities issuance or impose financial covenants. For Series A Notes and guarantees, including defaults, indenture amendments, and governing law, the text refers readers to the cited description.

Full Career Eligibility requires age/service thresholds, 180 days’ notice, professional service during notice, prior approval of continued vesting, and restrictions for 36 months on working in one’s profession or for a financial services company, with limited exceptions. If an eligible participant dies, a beneficiary or estate may receive shares calculated using completed-year performance and 100% payout for remaining years.

nodes.title: Continued Vesting: Government Office and Certification
nodes.summary: The page describes continued-vesting circumstances, including certain government, education, or nonprofit work; approved non-employee company directorships; and leaving employment for government office or candidacy. It also covers disability-related eligibility, required notice, documentation, and written Firm consent. Continued vesting generally requires a timely release, applicable advance notice and approvals, certification of compliance with employment restrictions, and compliance with the Award Agreement.

nodes.title: Death
nodes.summary: Upon death while eligible to vest, the designated beneficiary—or, absent a qualifying beneficiary, the estate—may receive shares calculated using completed-year average performance, one-third of target PSUs per completed performance year, and 100% payout for remaining years, plus dividend-equivalent shares through death. Distribution is due by the end of the following calendar year, usually registered within 60 days after required documents arrive. Award recipients also agree to obligations covering non-solicitation (with specified duration, limits, exceptions, and a California exclusion) and confidentiality during and after employment. Confidentiality rules define protected information, list exclusions, and preserve lawful disclosures, labor rights, and reporting or responding to legal and regulatory inquiries.

nodes.title: Death Benefits and Non-Solicitation Obligations
nodes.summary: Upon death, the beneficiary or estate receives dividend-equivalent shares based on equivalents through the death date, distributed by the end of the following calendar year; the Firm generally registers them within 60 days of receiving required documents. Award acceptance requires compliance with specified obligations. Non-solicitation restrictions apply during employment and for the longer of one year after termination or, if the award remains uncancelled, three years from the grant date. Without HR Director approval, they restrict soliciting current employees, hiring certain former employees, and soliciting or diverting covered business relationships, subject to stated exceptions. The restrictions do not apply to California work locations or authorized actions in ordinary employment duties.

nodes.title: • Confidentiality
nodes.summary: The agreement restricts disclosure or use of Firm confidential information during and after employment, while preserving legal reporting, labor rights, protected disclosures, and specified information exceptions; legally protected confidential information remains covered. Employees must give the Firm advance written notice, within five days of a demand or request when legally permitted, before responding to private-party employment inquiries and cooperate where lawful. It bars knowingly or recklessly false statements about the Firm and its people, requires cooperation with Firm investigations (with reasonable expense reimbursement), and permits government communications without Firm notice. Employees must provide compliance information and the Firm may disclose award terms to affected third parties. Applicable employment notice periods must be served, with possible paid leave and continued salary and benefits; the separate 180-day notice for full-career eligibility still applies. Up to all outstanding PSUs, including related units, may be cancelled at the Firm’s discretion for material harm, inaccurate performance metrics, employee misrepresentation, or grossly negligent failure to identify or raise material risks.

nodes.title: Employee Obligations and Notice Requirements
nodes.summary: Employees must notify the Firm within five days of legal demands or private requests for employment-related information, where lawful, and cooperate with related requests. They may not knowingly or recklessly make false statements about the Firm or its people, while retaining rights to report suspected legal violations and cooperate with authorities. Employees must assist with Firm investigations and litigation, with reasonable expenses reimbursed, and provide information needed to verify Award Agreement compliance; the Firm may disclose its terms to affected third parties. Applicable notice periods require advance written notice; the Firm may require continued service or paid leave, while employees remain loyal, professional, and exclusive and receive salary and certain benefits. The period may be mutually changed or waived, but the separate 180-day notice requirement for Full Career Eligibility remains applicable.

nodes.title: Remedies
nodes.summary: The Firm may cancel up to 100% of outstanding PSUs, including reinvested dividend equivalent units and calculated PSUs, for specified detrimental conduct, inaccurate performance metrics, misrepresentation, risk-management failures, actual or potential termination for Cause, failure to meet termination notice, cooperation, employment-restriction, or release-form requirements, or breach of other obligations. JPMorganChase may suspend vesting or share distribution while assessing cancellation, recovery, or distribution conditions; it is not liable for price changes during suspension, and suspended units may be reinstated under Plan procedures. See also the amendment and no-ownership-rights provisions.

nodes.title: • Recovery
nodes.summary: The Firm may recover up to the fair market value, at vesting or acceleration, of gross shares distributed under the award (including vested shares subject to holding requirements). Recovery may cover shares distributed within three years before notice for fraud or willful misconduct, violations of stated obligations, or post-employment restrictions on full-career eligibility or government office; or within one year for specified detrimental, risk-related conduct. Written or electronic notice—including notice that the Firm is evaluating recovery—preserves its rights, and a good-faith attempt to send notice to the last recorded address counts. Distributed shares include tax-withheld shares, but recovery excludes amounts the Firm determines reflect irrevocable, unrecoverable tax withholdings or payments. Repayment may be in shares or cash, is not a penalty, and does not limit other bonus-recoupment or incentive-compensation recovery obligations.

nodes.title: • Right to an Injunction
nodes.summary: A breach or attempted breach of the obligations is acknowledged to cause the Firm immediate, irreparable harm. The Firm is entitled to seek an injunction from a court of competent jurisdiction to stop any violation or further violation, in addition to any other remedies available at law or in equity.

nodes.title: Administrative Provisions
nodes.summary: The provisions cover tax withholding methods; setoff for debts with limits; PSU ownership, issuance, brokerage accounts, cancellation, and temporary share restrictions and recovery; binding successors and no employment or future-award rights; Section 409A timing; equitable adjustments for corporate changes and other circumstances; Committee authority, amendments, and severability; accelerated distribution or holding-period waivers for government ethics divestiture while preserving recovery obligations; personal-data processing, transfers, and authorization withdrawal; New York law, arbitration or exclusive federal forum, jury-trial and class-action waivers, and Firm attorney-fee recovery; non-transferability with inheritance exceptions; and application to existing outstanding equity awards.

title: Exhibit 19

nodes.title: 1. Summary or Rationale
nodes.summary: Exhibit 19 is JPMC’s firmwide Insider Trading Policy, effective February 12, 2026. It seeks to ensure compliance with U.S. securities laws by prohibiting Firm Personnel and Connected Persons from trading in Firm Securities while possessing Firm Material Nonpublic Information or improperly tipping others. It applies globally, subject to Firm policies, to Directors, Employees, Non-Employees, their relevant accounts, and accounts they can influence or control; JPMC and subsidiaries are also barred from trading while informed. Defined terms include JPMC’s CEO and CFO, Closed Window Period (outside an Open Window Period), and Connected Persons: a Firm Person’s spouse, domestic partner, minor children, financially supported persons, persons sharing investment decision authority, and entities controlled by them.

nodes.title: 2. Detailed Terms
nodes.summary: Exhibit 19 is JPMC’s firmwide Insider Trading Policy, effective February 12, 2026. It aims to prevent trading in Firm Securities while possessing Firm material nonpublic information (MNPI) and unlawful tipping. It covers directors, employees, non-employees, their connected persons and relevant accounts worldwide, and prohibits JPMC and subsidiaries from trading while possessing MNPI. It defines covered persons and connected persons; Firm, securities and MNPI; open and closed trading windows; window-list personnel; trading and transactions; and related terms, including officers, entities, plans, instruments and regulatory references. Open windows generally run from the day after quarterly earnings release through the 15th of the following month, but may be suspended; window-list personnel are notified when designated.

nodes.title: 3. Prohibition on Insider Trading
nodes.summary: Insider trading is illegal and prohibited. Firm Personnel and Connected Persons, as well as JPMC and its subsidiaries, must not trade in Firm Securities while possessing Firm MNPI. When JPMC possesses or may be deemed to possess such information, it generally observes a trading blackout, except that it may repurchase common stock under a 10b5-1 Plan during the blackout before quarterly earnings announcements.

nodes.title: 4. Prohibition on Unauthorized Disclosure
nodes.summary:
4. Prohibition on Unauthorized Disclosure
Firm Personnel and their Connected Persons must not impermissibly provide Firm MNPI to any person who may trade on the basis of that information (i.e., “tipping”). Inaddition, Firm MNPI must not be shared with any person unless the disclosure complies with the Firm’s policies concerning the safeguarding of confidential information, including the Code of Conduct.

nodes.title: 5. Policies applicable to Window List Personnel
nodes.summary: Window List Personnel are those with potential access to Firm MNPI and are notified by email. They and their Connected Persons may trade Firm Securities only during Open Window Periods with Compliance preapproval; approvals are time-limited, windows may be suspended, and rare exceptions may be granted with manager, Compliance, and Legal consultation. Non-Window List Personnel generally lack these preapproval and holding-period requirements, subject to other restrictions; certain personnel must always preclear JPMC transactions. Covered transactions include purchases, sales, gifts, plan liquidations, limit orders, 10b5-1 Plans, and certain option-related share uses. Specified automatic purchases, approved-plan transactions, and certain orders or derivatives are exempt from preapproval; employee options and SARs have additional restrictions. Corporate Officers and Directors must use 10b5-1 Plans for open-market sales; specified exercises, gifts, GRATs, and trust transfers require preapproval but not a plan. Plans require preapproval, compliance with Rule 10b5-1(c) and applicable share-retention policies, and may be created, amended, or terminated only during an Open Window Period.

nodes.title: 6. Policies applicable to Corp Officers and Directors
nodes.summary: Restricted activities include liquidating Firm Securities, changing limit orders, creating/amending/terminating 10b5-1 Plans, and using owned JPMC shares or withholding shares for option exercises, subject to an exception for plans established during an Open Window; additional rules apply to employee options and SARs. Exempt transactions include qualifying preapproved dividend reinvestments and automatic purchases, transactions under qualifying 10b5-1 Plans, and orders or derivatives placed during an Open Window but executed during a Closed Window. Corporate Officers and Directors must use a 10b5-1 Plan for open-market sales; exercising and holding awards, charitable gifts, and specified GRAT or trust transactions require preapproval but not a plan. Plans must satisfy Rule 10b5-1(c), comply with share-retention policies, and be entered, amended, or terminated only during Open Windows. During Open Windows, required trades and plan actions need designated approvals: generally CEO and GC; GC actions require CEO approval, Firmwide Controller actions GC and CFO approval, and CEO actions GC approval. Corporate Officer approvals also go to Compliance, and generally expire at the end of the next business day unless specified otherwise.

nodes.title: 7. Other Prohibitions
nodes.summary: The policy prohibits Window List and other personally restricted personnel from trading Firm Securities through forwards, futures, swaps, uncovered options (except LEAPS), or short sales. Direct hedging is allowed only when proportionate and fully covered. All employees may not hedge or pledge unvested deferred compensation or vested JPMC stock subject to a holding restriction. JPMC Operating Committee members and directors may not pledge or hedge JPMC shares they own or hold through deferred compensation. Window List Personnel and Connected Persons must meet region- or business-specific minimum holding periods; vested JPMC shares and ESPP-purchased shares are deemed to satisfy them.

nodes.title: 8. Post-termination Transactions
nodes.summary: After leaving the Firm, anyone aware of Firm material nonpublic information, including connected persons, must not trade Firm securities or disclose the information until it becomes public or immaterial. Personnel and connected persons bear responsibility for compliance; the policy does not guarantee legal compliance, provide legal advice, or shield anyone from liability, and financial emergencies are no excuse. Violations may bring civil or criminal liability and discipline up to termination, subject to local law; the Firm may require trades to be canceled at the individual’s expense. Questions should go to Compliance or the Office of the Secretary, and personnel should consult the Code of Conduct and related policies.

nodes.title: 9. Personal Responsibility and Disciplinary Action
nodes.summary: The text prohibits hedging or pledging JPMC stock acquired through vested RSUs where local remuneration rules impose restrictions. Operating Committee members and directors may not pledge or hedge JPMC shares they own or hold through deferred compensation. Window List Personnel and connected persons must observe region- or business-specific minimum holding periods; vested shares and ESPP-purchased shares meet this requirement. After leaving the Firm, anyone aware of material nonpublic information must not trade or disclose it until it is public or no longer material. Individuals remain personally responsible for compliance; the policy does not guarantee immunity from liability or provide legal advice, and financial emergencies are no excuse. Violations may bring reminders, disciplinary action up to termination, or instructions to cancel trades at the individual’s expense. Questions should go to Compliance or the Office of the Secretary, and personnel should consult the Code of Conduct and related policies.
